Our findings inform the design of gaze-informed adaptive disclosure interfaces that dynamically adjust transparency levels based on readers' attentional patterns and news context.

title: Knowledge Lineage from Isnad to AI: Reframing Authorship and Responsibility in the Generative AI Era
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming scholarly writing and research, raising urgent questions about authorship, intellectual ownership, and epistemic responsibility.This study aims to investigate how knowledge lineage-defined as the traceable chain of transmission, transformation, and attribution-connecting ideas to their origins-can be preserved in an era where AI increasingly mediates knowledge production.Adopting a theoretical-conceptual methodology, the paper integrates Western philosophy (Foucault's author-function, Kuhn's paradigm shifts), Floridi's concept of ectypes, and Islamic epistemology (isnād, amāna, mas'ūliyya), alongside comparative analysis of institutional practices at Harvard, Oxford, and King Saud University.The analysis reveals that while AI accelerates content creation, it simultaneously introduces epistemic opacity, breaks attribution chains, and generates "orphaned" knowledge outputs that lack identifiable provenance.To address these risks, the study proposes a multi-tiered ethical framework that includes mandatory AI-use disclosure, human-in-the-loop verification, metadata-based "AI isnād," and institutional accountability mechanisms.This framework bridges global AI ethics (OECD, UNESCO) with culturally embedded models of moral responsibility, reinforcing that human scholars must remain the ethical custodians of knowledge.The paper concludes that preserving knowledge lineage is not merely a technical challenge but a moral and cultural imperative.By embedding transparency, traceability, and accountability into both technical systems and institutional policies, the integrity of scholarly communication can be sustained in an AI-saturated future.
venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences

title: Large language models as information providers for appropriate antimicrobial use: computational text analysis and expert-rated comparison of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Antimicrobial resistance is a critical public health threat. Large language models (LLMs) show great capability for providing health information. This study evaluates the effectiveness of LLMs in providing information on antibiotic use and infection management. METHODS: Using a mixed-method approach, responses to healthcare expert-designed scenarios from ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, Claude 2.0 and Gemini 1.0, in both Italian and English, were analysed. Computational text analysis assessed readability, lexical diversity and sentiment, while content quality was assessed by three experts via DISCERN tool. RESULTS: 16 scenarios were developed. A total of 101 outputs and 5454 Likert-scale (1-5) scores were obtained for the analysis. A general positive performance gradient was found from ChatGPT 3.5 and 4.0 to Claude to Gemini. Gemini, although producing only five outputs before self-inhibition, consistently outperformed the other models across almost all metrics, producing more detailed, accessible, varied content and a positive overtone. ChatGPT 4.0 demonstrated the highest lexical diversity. A difference in performance by language was observed. All models showed a median score of 1 (IQR=2) regarding the domain addressing antimicrobial resistance. DISCUSSION: The study highlights a positive performance gradient towards Gemini, which showed superior content quality, accessibility and contextual awareness, although acknowledging its smaller dataset. Generating appropriate content to address antimicrobial resistance proved challenging. CONCLUSIONS: LLMs offer great promise to provide appropriate medical information. However, they should play a supporting role rather than representing a replacement option for medical professionals, confirming the need for expert oversight and improved artificial intelligence design.

title: Ethical Risks and Point-of-Use Governance of AI in IPE: Insights from Interviews with 17 Instructors
abstract: This study examines ethical risks and workable governance for artificial intelligence in university ideological and political education in China. Semi-structured interviews with 17 instructors from five universities in Chongqing conducted from March to June 2025 were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Six themes characterize current practice: privacy and consent remain fragile in attendance, proctoring, and analytics; the teacher role shifts from authority to curator and ethical gatekeeper; recommendation and moderation shape visibility and the continuity of deliberation; assessment integrity benefits from process-based evidence and explicit disclosure; metric-driven activity targets can crowd out value reasoning; and governance and accountability depend on institutional capacity and consistent rules. The findings indicate that responsible integration requires governance at the point of use across classroom, platform, and institution, including course-level disclosure and granular consent, explainable moderation with instructor overrides and traceability, process-based assessment with AI-use disclosure, curated corpora linked to retrieval-augmented generation with citation binding, routine audits, and faculty training.

title: RE: Clinician- and facility-level factors associated with chemotherapy dose reductions in stages I-IIIA breast cancer
abstract: To the Editor: We read with great interest the article by Sampathkumar et al. examining clinician- and facility-level correlates of chemotherapy dose reductions in stages I-IIIA breast cancer.1 Their use of detailed regimen-level electronic health record data within a large integrated care system is a notable strength. We are concerned, however, that the discussion moves too quickly from association to practice recommendation. The central issue is that lower frequencies of first-cycle dose proportion (FCDP) reduction or average relative dose intensity (ARDI) reduction cannot be assumed to indicate better chemotherapy delivery. The authors appropriately acknowledge that they were unable to determine whether dose modifications were clinically appropriate because laboratory data, toxicity measures, and patient-reported outcomes were unavailable, and early discontinuation was not captured. In our view, this limitation is foundational rather than secondary. If clinically justified dose attenuation cannot be separated from undertreatment, then clinician or facility characteristics associated with less reduction should not be interpreted as markers of more optimal practice. A related concern is the interpretation of ARDI as a prescribing construct. ARDI is better understood as a composite delivery metric because it may reflect several pathways, including dose reduction, treatment delay, and incomplete treatment completion.2-4 This distinction matters for the proposed explanation of lower ARDI in less urban facilities, where the authors invoke access barriers, scheduling constraints, and delayed toxicity management. Such mechanisms may reduce ARDI without necessarily reflecting a different clinician dosing philosophy. Residual confounding may also be more consequential than the discussion suggests. Although the models adjusted for major clinical covariates, key determinants of dose modification were unavailable, including functional status, baseline hematologic and organ reserve, growth-factor support, early toxic effects, transportation burden, and social support. Several clinician- and facility-level variables may therefore act primarily as proxies for patient complexity and supportive-care capacity rather than as independent drivers of dosing decisions. Accordingly, we believe these findings are best viewed as hypothesis-generating. Before recommending subspecialization or practice restructuring to increase volume or practice size, future analyses should distinguish upfront dose reduction, treatment delay, and early discontinuation, and should evaluate toxicity, guideline concordance, and patient outcomes. Without that additional context, less dose reduction should not be presumed to represent better care. AI use disclosure: ChatGPT was used only to assist with language editing, drafting support, sentence refinement, and formatting of this correspondence. ChatGPT was not used for study design, data analysis, data interpretation, reference verification, or generation of original scientific content. The authors reviewed, verified, and approved the final manuscript and take full responsibility for its content. Sheng Yu (Conceptualization, Investigation, Methodology, Writing—original draft, Writing—review & editing), Xiushen Wang (Investigation, Validation, Writing—review & editing), and Hong Ge (Conceptualization, Methodology, Writing—review & editing) No funding was used for this study. The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare. No new data were generated or analyzed for this correspondence.
venue: JNCI Journal of the National Cancer Institute

title: Empowering pre-service teachers with generative AI: a GenAI-TPACK-based approach to digital storytelling
abstract: This qualitative study adopts an experience-oriented design informed by phenomenological principles to explore pre-service primary teachers’ experiences with AI-supported digital storytelling. Going beyond the traditional TPACK framework, the study is grounded in the recently proposed GenAI-TPACK model, highlighting the evolving interaction of technological, pedagogical, content, and ethical domains. It investigates how teacher candidates integrated generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Suno AI into storytelling practices aligned with national curriculum objectives. The participants included 40 second-year pre-service teachers at a public university in Türkiye during the 2024–2025 academic year. Data were collected via a Google Forms-based open-ended response form and reflective reports. Digital stories were used to contextualize the learning process, but they were not systematically analyzed. The analysis was conducted using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings indicate that participants reported enhancements in creative thinking, narrative development, and multimodal literacy. Candidates used AI for plot generation, visual and audio design, and curriculum-aligned instructional planning, yet they also encountered challenges related to prompt clarity, language precision, and ethical considerations (e.g., copyright and data use). Overall, the experience fostered reflective pedagogical thinking and supported the design of innovative, curriculum-relevant, and ethically informed learning activities. This study contributes to teacher education by showing how pre-service teachers used GenAI-TPACK-related knowledge within a scaffolded 14-week digital storytelling course, particularly when making prompt-mediated design decisions, iteratively refining multimodal outputs, and attending to ethical considerations such as copyright and responsible use. Pre-service teachers used GenAI tools for creative and curriculum-aligned storytelling. The GenAI-TPACK framework supported the integration of AI in authentic pedagogy. Participants adapted AI-generated content based on students’ developmental needs. Ethical awareness and copyright sensitivity emerged as active pedagogical concerns. GenAI tools functioned as digital collaborators, not just technical assistants.

title: Authors self-disclosed use of artificial intelligence in research submissions to 49 biomedical journals: A cross-sectional study
abstract: ABSTRACT OBJECTIVE To analyze the frequency of self-disclosed use of AI in research manuscripts submitted to 49 biomedical journals and to identify types of AI tools used, the tasks they assisted with, and factors associated with disclosure. DESIGN Cross-sectional study. SETTING 49 biomedical journals published by BMJ Group. PARTICIPANTS Submitting authors of 25,114 empirical research manuscripts including systematic reviews and meta-analyses, submitted between 8 April 2024 and 6 November 2024. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Prevalence of manuscripts with self-disclosed use of AI, types of AI tools used, the tasks they assisted with and factors associated with disclosure. RESULTS There was a total of 25,114 eligible submissions: Asia (13,505; 53.8%), Europe (6,523; 26.0%), North America (2,795; 11.1%), Africa (1,196; 4.8%), Oceania (708; 2.8%), and South America (387; 1.5%). A total of 1,431 submissions (5.7%) disclosed the use of AI. The most frequently reported AI tools used were Generative AI Chatbots (812/1431; 56.7%) and writing assistants (182; 12.7%). The majority of authors who disclosed AI use reported using it to improve the quality of their writing (1,248/1,431; 87%). Additionally, translation (107; 7.5%), generating data and output (87, 6.1%), literature searches (49; 3.4%), analyzing data (31; 2.2%), image processing or analysis (49; 3.4%), code writing (15; 1.0%), and managing references (14; 0.9%) were mentioned as tasks AI assisted with. Authors from South America (OR=1.75; 95%-CI: 1.22-2.49) and Europe (OR=1.28; 95%-CI: 1.14-1.45) were significantly more likely to disclose AI use than those from Asia. Conversely, each additional author reduced disclosure odds by 1% (OR=0.99, 95%-CI: 0.97-0.99). Acceptance rate, impact factor, type of journal, and peer review model) were not associated with AI use disclosure. CONCLUSIONS We found that only a small proportion (5.7%) of submitting authors disclosed AI use, which is substantially lower than proportions reported in surveys. Improving the quality of writing was the primarily task AI assisted with and AI Chatbots were the most commonly disclosed tool. Authors may be uncertain about what AI use requires disclosure or may be hesitant to declare it. What is already known on this topic ▪ Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in the conduct of scientific research and writing of publications and the way it is used is changing rapidly. ▪ Leading publishers and editorial organizations dedicated to promoting integrity and best practices in academic publishing have issued policies requiring authors to disclose all AI use in their content. ▪ Previous surveys show that a substantial proportion of researchers (28% to 76%) say they have used AI in their research. What this study adds ▪ This study of a process for mandatory declaration of AI use in research manuscripts submitted to 49 biomedical journals found a prevalence of only 5.7%, which is substantially lower than use reported in surveys. ▪ Improving the quality of writing was the most common reported task performed by AI, and g enerative AI Chatbots are the most frequently disclosed AI tool used. How this study might affect research, practice or policy ▪ Current mandatory questions on AI use may have only limited value and other measures are needed to improve declaration and to support detection of undisclosed use.

title: “Transparency is More Than a Label”: Audiences’ Information Needs for AI Use Disclosures in News
abstract: This study evaluates the role of disclosure transparency in rebuilding trust in journalism amid the increasing integration of generative AI (GenAI) tools in news production. While AI technologies enhance journalistic workflows by automating and augmenting content creation, they also introduce opacity in professional decisions, complicating traditional disclosure transparency norms and its practices. The paper maps citizens' perceptions regarding disclosure transparency of AI use in journalism, addressing two key themes: (1) the practical information needs of news consumers about AI-generated content and (2) the specific rationales when exposed to (disclosures of) AI-generated news content. Through qualitative focus groups (N = 21), the exploratory research reveals a strong demand for clear, visible, and detailed disclosures about AI-generated content. Participants emphasized the necessity of including general source references akin to traditional authorship attributions, explicitly stating AI involvement - for example, a label such as 'generated by AI' alongside author and publication details. Visual indicators like logos or watermarks in contrasting colors were preferred to ensure AI disclosures are noticeable and not easily overlooked. This study contributes to developing more granular audience-centered, practical guidelines for AI transparency in journalism that goes beyond the mere 'label', emphasizing that effective disclosure transparency requires more than simply 'informing' audiences.

title: Will your AI turn backers away? Evidence from Kickstarter's AI-use disclosure policy
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how creative work is produced, raising new questions about authenticity, originality, and human effort in entrepreneurial settings. We examine how platform-mandated AI-use disclosure is associated with crowdfunding outcomes, using Kickstarter’s 2023 disclosure policy and a dataset of over 63,000 campaigns launched between 2022 and 2024. Drawing on signaling theory, we argue that an AI-use label functions as a platform-governed cue that backers may interpret as signaling reduced human effort, potentially shaping how they evaluate creators and campaigns. Empirically, we find that AI-use disclosure is associated with a significantly lower likelihood of campaign success, with this negative association concentrated in reduced backer participation. The disclosure penalty is weaker when campaign descriptions are more subjective and easier to read, but stronger in technology-oriented campaigns where human expertise and originality are especially salient. It is also weaker for creators with stronger prior track records. Our findings identify AI-use disclosure as a novel platform-governed signal in crowdfunding, contribute to research on how platform-designed information environments shape user evaluations, and highlight potential unintended consequences of AI transparency requirements for platform design and policy.

title: Adaptation and Psychometric Properties of the Test for Instagram Addiction (TIA) Among Nursing and Midwifery Students in Clinical Learning Environments
abstract: Background: In recent years, excessive use of Instagram among students, particularly those in nursing and midwifery, has increased and is associated with compulsive behaviors, reduced self-control, and negative consequences. This can disrupt their concentration, clinical decision-making, and professional interactions. Objectives: This study aims to culturally adapt and validate the Test for Instagram Addiction (TIA) for use among nursing and midwifery students in clinical learning environments in Iran. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among nursing and midwifery students in clinical training hospitals in Kerman, Iran. The TIA was translated via a two-phase approach involving bilingual translators and experts in psychometrics, medical sciences, and linguistics. The instrument underwent content validity testing through expert evaluations and construct validation via exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis (EFA and CFA). Reliability was assessed via internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha) and test–retest methods. Concurrent validity was examined by correlating TIA scores with scores from the General Phubbing Scale (GPS). The sample consisted of 400 students for EFA, 300 for CFA, and additional samples for reliability assessments. Results: The TIA demonstrated high content validity, with content validity ratios (CVRs) between 0.80 and 1.00 and content validity indices (CVIs) ranging from 0.83 to 0.97, indicating clarity, relevance, and alignment with the intended construct. The exploratory factor analysis identified six factors consistent with the original scale, namely, lack of control, disengagement, escapism, health and interpersonal troubles, excessive use, and obsession, explaining 65.3% of the total variance. The CFA confirmed the model’s good fit to the data, with fit indices exceeding the recommended thresholds. Reliability tests indicated excellent internal consistency (α = 0.919) and good test–retest reliability (r = 0.89, P < 0.01). Concurrent validity was confirmed through a strong positive correlation with the GPS score (r = 0.76, P < 0.01). Conclusions: The Persian TIA is a valid and reliable tool for assessing Instagram addiction in nursing and midwifery students in clinical settings and is recommended for use in research and clinical interventions.
venue: Iranian Journal of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences

title: Generative AI use before medical visits: disclosure-item responses, trust, and care-seeking behaviors in a cross-sectional social-media survey in Poland
abstract: Background Patient-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used for health information seeking, yet their role in patient–physician communication remains insufficiently characterized. Using the Network Episode Model as the primary framework, this study examined self-reported pre-consultation AI use, whether respondents reported disclosing that use to a physician, and self-reported AI-associated health-behavior change in a convenience sample of Polish adults recruited via social media. Findings are exploratory. Methods Cross-sectional online survey, anonymous with respect to the investigators ( N = 1,044), administered in Polish via Google Forms with programmed routing; recruitment used a multi-account social-media strategy. A 24-item de novo questionnaire assessed health-related and pre-consultation AI use, disclosure-item responses, trust, self-reported behavioral consequences, and sociodemographics. Q13 responses were analyzed among respondents reporting AI use before a medical visit; the survey did not confirm that a consultation subsequently occurred. Exploratory analyses included chi-square, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman correlations, and logistic regression restricted to definite Yes/No responses; the originally submitted coding and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment were retained as sensitivity analyses. Results Health-related AI use was reported by 84.3% ( n = 880; 95% CI 82.0–86.4). Among respondents reporting AI use before a medical visit ( n = 519), 82.5% ( n = 428; 95% CI 79.0–85.5) selected ‘No’ when asked whether they had informed a physician about that use. Because attendance was not confirmed, this proportion cannot be interpreted as a rate of what patients withheld during completed clinical encounters. Selection of ‘No’ was similar across visit-avoidance strata (79.2–86.8%). Among those selecting ‘No’ who reported no AI-related visit avoidance ( n = 235), the most frequent reasons were fear of a negative physician reaction (86.4%) and reluctance to undermine physician authority (74.9%). In primary definite-response models, male gender and greater AI trust were associated with the outcomes; AI trust was strongly negatively associated with age. Apparent discrimination and explained variation were modest. Conclusions Most respondents reporting pre-consultation AI use selected ‘No’ on the disclosure item. Because consultation attendance and a defined index episode were not confirmed, the actual disclosure rate within completed clinical encounters cannot be estimated from this survey. The findings advance a hypothesis about a possible communication barrier requiring prospective, episode-based study.

title: Digital Tools for Academic Writing: A Systematic Analysis of AI and Technology-Enhanced Support
abstract: This study provides a comprehensive analysis of digital tools supporting the academic writing and publication process, examining AI-powered, AI-assisted, and technology-enhanced platforms available to researchers. Using document analysis, 46 tools were identified and evaluated in ten functional groups: brainstorming tools, research assistants, writing assistants, translation tools, grammar and style checkers, plagiarism detectors, citation tools, data visualization tools, document formatting tools, and collaboration platforms. Analysis reveals that technology-enhanced tools (37%) remain prevalent alongside AI-assisted (43%) and AI-powered tools (20%), with each category serving distinct functions in the research process. While these tools offer significant benefits including enhanced productivity, improved linguistic accuracy, streamlined citation management, and support for collaborative work, critical challenges emerged including cost barriers (subscription models dominating 87% of tools), algorithmic bias affecting non-native English speakers, concerns about over-reliance on AI-generated content, and implementation gaps with most institutions lacking clear usage guidelines. The study provides practical recommendations for tool selection across different research stages, emphasizing the need for researchers to critically evaluate outputs, maintain transparency through appropriate disclosure, and balance technological assistance with development of core academic writing skills. These findings contribute to understanding the current state of AI-powered academic writing tools and provide evidence-based guidance for researchers, institutions, and publishers.

title: Promoting Academic Integrity through Generative AI-Use Disclosure: A Single-Case Study from an Argentine University
Artificial intelligence tools in scholarly publishing: guidance for peer reviewers
abstract: An Academic Medicine Podcast episode featuring this article is available from Apple Podcasts (https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/academic-medicine-podcast/id1112697692) or wherever you get your podcasts. Peer review is fundamental to ensuring research excellence and integrity in scholarly publishing and serves as a mechanism for knowledge building in academic medicine.1,2 High-quality peer review brings relevant expertise to the evaluation of scholarship and has been demonstrated to improve manuscripts under consideration, benefitting both authors and editors.2,3 Peer review also acts as a crucial safeguard for rigor and helps minimize bias in the published literature.4 Moreover, engaging in peer review nurtures the professional development of reviewers themselves, sharpening critical appraisal skills and deepening their understanding of current and emerging conversations in the field.1,2 Peer review is, nevertheless, a time-intensive professional activity, and peer reviewers themselves have increasingly become a limited resource.5,6 The proliferation of journals, steady rise in manuscript submissions, and increasing demand for rapid decision-making and publication have placed an unprecedented strain on peer review. Concerns related to an inadequate number of expert peer reviewers, the quality and brevity of reviews, and reviewer fatigue are now common.7 These challenges place a burden on peer-review processes and threaten their role and sustainability in scholarly publishing.5 Consequently, the need to develop innovative approaches to peer review is increasingly clear. In this context, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) presents both opportunities and dilemmas for scholars, reviewers, editors, and societal stakeholders. For example, recent findings8 from a survey of more than 5000 researchers revealed that nearly half consider it acceptable to involve generative AI in peer review, and most support the use of AI tools to assist reviewers. Yet, 60% oppose the idea of AI drafting full review reports as a replacement for human expert-generated reports, citing concerns about confidentiality and trust. These findings highlight novel ethical tensions for journal editors, who rely on peer review to help inform the evaluation of scholarly work. As reviewers experiment with AI tools to ease workload and improve efficiency, the ways in which AI is used by peer reviewers have broad implications. At a systems level, for instance, the unfettered use of AI in peer review could introduce unvetted or potentially erroneous material into the same databases that AI models draw upon, compounding misinformation and potentially undermining the credibility of scientific communication for society at large.9 In addition, issues of author consent, protection of identifiable data, intellectual property rights, and other ethical safeguards remain undefined.10 These challenges thus raise important questions for all stakeholders in the development and publication of scholarship, including authors, reviewers, editors, readers, and the public. Might there be appropriate, narrowly defined, and practical applications of AI that enhance, rather than erode, the peer-review process? What practices can be put in place to ensure that engagement of AI facilitates well-informed, rigorous, and fair-minded reviews? Could AI help reduce reviewer fatigue, augment expertise, enhance feedback quality, and strengthen scholarly work? Or will its use compromise confidentiality, introduce bias, and ultimately erode the trust that underpins the peer-review process? Given the rapid evolution of AI and the novel challenges it presents for academic publishing, we at Academic Medicine and MedEdPORTAL have adopted a principle-driven approach to guide the use of AI in peer review. The principles of professional accountability, confidentiality, fair-mindedness and avoidance of harm, and transparency serve as the framework for our approach. The journals’ policy on AI use for peer review appears in Box 1, with examples of appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI provided in Table 1. Our aim in developing this framework is to anchor reviewer practices in shared values, enabling reviewers to thoughtfully adopt tools that are genuinely useful while preserving the integrity and role of expert peer review. Our intention is thus not to prohibit the use of AI, but rather to provide clear guidance and structure for peer reviewers and the range of stakeholders of our journals so that its integration enhances, rather than compromises, the rigor and trust that define our scholarly work. Examples of appropriate and inappropriate uses of artificial intelligence (AI) for peer reviewers. Examples of appropriate and inappropriate uses of artificial intelligence (AI) for peer reviewers. Peer reviewers are accountable, as individuals with specialized expertise, as members of a profession, and as human beings, for the quality and integrity of their evaluations of their colleagues’ scholarship. Concretely, this accountability means that reviewers should comment only on scholarship that falls within their area of expertise and refrain from commenting on work outside their scope of knowledge. For example, peer reviewers may find it useful to use AI tools to retrieve recent literature to inform or strengthen their understanding of a topic. However, AI should not be used as a substitute for a reviewer’s own scholarly judgment or disciplinary expertise. As members of a profession, peer reviewers are expected to conduct their reviews in a manner that respects the imperative for excellence and trustworthiness in science and scholarship more broadly. This professional expectation includes demonstrating respect for their colleagues whose work is being reviewed. In this context, some have advocated a “golden rule” approach in which reviewers should only use AI in ways that they would hope and expect others to use AI when evaluating their own work.10 And, while it may seem self-evident, it is important to emphasize that peer reviewers are humans. An AI tool cannot assume, or be assigned, professional accountability.11 Just as authors must be human, so too must peer reviewers. To demonstrate professional accountability, peer reviewers are expected to engage directly with manuscripts under review and to apply their own scholarly judgment in formulating comments and recommendations. They should limit AI assistance to acceptable uses (see Box 1) that do not involve uploading confidential materials or outsourcing evaluation. Reviewers must accept full responsibility for the accuracy of their reviews submitted and be prepared to address editor questions about the origin of their comments or any practices that could limit or bias the review. Importantly, professional accountability includes being truthful in disclosing whether and how AI was used in their conduct of the peer review. Academic Medicine and MedEdPORTAL adhere to the Committee on Publication Ethics12 and the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors13 guidance regarding peer review. This guidance is unequivocal. Reviewers must treat all author materials (eg, abstracts, figures, full texts) under review as strictly confidential and not share them without permission. Confidentiality is essential to the integrity of peer review because it protects authors’ unpublished ideas and data, preserves trust in the review process, and protects intellectual property from exposure or misuse. In simplest terms, just as a physician should not read a patient’s clinical records aloud in an elevator, a peer reviewer should not share the contents of an unpublished manuscript with others. The same standard applies in digital or physical environments, where confidentiality could be compromised. Authors submit their manuscripts to a journal with the expectation that the submission materials will be treated as confidential. This principle of confidentiality extends to the use of AI tools. Uploading any portion of a manuscript under review into an AI tool risks breaching confidentiality. Such actions risk exposing authors’ intellectual property to third-party servers where it may be stored, accessed by others, or used for future model training. There can be no guarantee of how AI tools will use materials once they have been uploaded, which carries the potential for misuse of author materials and the introduction of weak or biased data, analyses, and interpretations into public models that will serve as the basis of subsequent AI-generated content. While some institutions offer “closed” systems, which claim not to train on uploaded content or feed it into public models, they can also pose risks (eg, internal data circulation or system logging). For this reason, reviewers must not upload author materials under review to any AI tool, whether it is closed or open. Peer review should be based on expertise and fair-minded assessment and should not be delegated to AI tools. While AI may help with mechanical tasks like clarifying grammar, organizing notes, or summarizing a reviewer’s own comments, the intellectual work of assessing a manuscript’s originality, significance, methodology, and implications of the work are nontransferable responsibilities and rest with the human reviewer. Reviewers should approach their work in a neutral and balanced manner and seek to minimize sources of bias that may affect their assessment of scholarship. Fair-mindedness in peer review is an intentional effort to minimize bias. It is essential as a safeguard against harm that may occur when flawed or erroneous work is published or when contributions are undervalued due to implicit bias or uneven standards. Related to this, because AI tools are trained on uneven corpora, they may perpetuate or amplify existing biases in scholarship,14–17 threatening a fair-minded evaluation of a manuscript. In relying on AI, peer reviewers may introduce distortions, including bias from underlying datasets as well as erroneous information and AI “hallucinations.” To uphold fairness and avoid harm, peer reviewers should be cautious in how they engage with AI-generated content. They must be on guard for ways in which AI might shape their judgment, whether by skewing it due to counterfactual information or errors of emphasis or by disadvantaging particular research topics, methodologies, authors, or populations under study. Transparency is essential in maintaining trust and accountability in peer review. Peer reviewers have a responsibility to disclose whether and how AI tools contributed to a review. Clear disclosure allows editors to interpret a review in its full context and maintains trust in the fairness and rigor of the process. While transparency is always appreciated, not all uses of AI require disclosure, though this may evolve as AI tools and related publishing standards continue to develop. For example, currently, routine language editing (eg, spell check, grammar check) performed by AI tools does not require disclosure. More substantive uses of AI tools, however, such as rephrasing for clarity, generating an outline, summarizing publicly available information, or translating text, may be acceptable when appropriately disclosed to the editor. On the other hand, certain uses of AI, even when disclosed in a transparent manner, are never acceptable. For example, uploading confidential author materials in AI systems or delegating evaluative judgments to AI violates both confidentiality and accountability. Such unacceptable practices can compromise the trust that the scholarly community places in its reviewers and that society places in science. As editors and reviewers navigate the evolution of AI tools in academic publishing, the challenge is not merely to decide whether AI should be used in peer review, but how AI can be integrated in ways that uphold excellence in scholarship and trustworthiness in academia. The promise of AI is undeniable. When used appropriately, it aligns with the core purpose of peer review: to improve scholarship through thoughtful, expert evaluation. At the same time, the dilemmas posed by AI use in peer review are profound. Relying on AI to generate language or analysis introduces uncertainty about confidentiality, authorship, accountability, and bias. These concerns underscore the need for transparency and editorial oversight to ensure that peer review remains both rigorous and trustworthy. Together, the principles of professional accountability, confidentiality, fair-mindedness and avoidance of harm, and transparency provide a framework for responsible AI use in peer review. As AI tools continue to evolve, application of these principles will ensure that peer review remains rooted in human expertise, judgment, and integrity. Moving forward, we can imagine a future in which authors may opt to allow their manuscripts to be securely processed by journal-controlled AI systems, enabling both higher-quality and more sustainable peer review. Properly designed, such systems might help reviewers identify inconsistencies, highlight relevant literature, or check adherence to methodologic rigor and reporting guidelines—while remaining under the supervision of humans who are accountable for the work. We recognize our own responsibility to remain informed as the field evolves. Along the way, all journals must remain committed to the same principles that should guide reviewers. As AI tools are developed and tested to contribute to peer review in ethical, legitimate ways, editors always remain accountable for every editorial decision rendered. Author materials must continue to be protected as confidential, and authors must have the opportunity to opt into or out of any AI tools used by journals. To ensure fair-mindedness and avoidance of harm in editorial decision-making, editors will need to understand the potential weaknesses or biases of AI tools intended to support peer review and actively work to mitigate these. Finally, editors must be transparent with authors and reviewers about any changes to policies or practices about the use of AI in peer review. The availability and sophistication of these tools are quickly evolving, and journal editors must recognize when it is time to consider principle-driven changes to existing approaches. As AI tools become more sophisticated and embedded in scholarly work, journals will need to clarify expectations and provide equitable access to approved, secure tools to avoid creating new divides between reviewers who have access to advanced systems and those who do not. Realizing these possibilities will require not only technological innovation but also shared ethical commitments. For now, however, the responsible path is clear: AI tools may have narrow uses to help reviewers express their assessments of manuscripts but must never replace the expertise, judgment, and trust that define the peer-review process. Use of AI Tools in Peer Review: Academic Medicine and MedEdPORTAL Policy Reviewers have professional obligations regarding AI use, disclosure, and attestation. Author materials (eg, manuscripts, abstracts, figures, tables, appendices) under review are confidential and remain the intellectual property of the authors. Just as reviewers must not share any portion of these materials with any person, except in rare circumstances and only with the permission of the editor-in-chief, reviewers must not upload materials from authors into an AI system. Accordingly, the use of generative AI tools (eg, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) to analyze materials and/or to generate the contents of a review is prohibited. Authors should not use generative AI tools as a replacement for their own scope of expertise, knowledge, or judgment relevant to their evaluation of the materials. The journals recognize that some reviewers may wish to use AI tools to improve the grammar or readability of their own review. This use is permitted, provided the reviewer uploads only their own original work (ie, their own reviewer comments) and no identifiable information from the authors’ materials is included. Upon submitting a review, reviewers are required to disclose whether they have used AI tools in preparing their review. Reviewers are required to attest that no author materials were uploaded to AI tools, including publicly available as well as private or institution-based AI systems, and that the substance of their review was not generated by such tools. Only a human reviewer can be accountable for a submitted review, and reviewers are required to attest that they accept responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of their review. K. Roberts is editor-in-chief of Academic Medicine. The opinions expressed in this editorial do not necessarily reflect the opinions of the AAMC or its members.

title: Exploring the ideologies of English on a Taiwan-based online tutoring platform
abstract: As English has attained unprecedented global status, studies have shown that language ideologies surrounding English learning and teaching can contribute to discrimination against non-native English speakers and non-standard varieties. While previous research has mainly examined the reproduction of such ideologies in physical classrooms, online English-learning platforms remain underexplored. This study addresses that gap by investigating ideologies of English in social-media promotional materials produced by a popular Taiwan-based online tutoring platform. A dataset of 116 short tutoring videos from the platform’s Instagram and YouTube accounts was analyzed using content analysis and critical discourse analysis. The findings identify four recurring ideological themes: (1) structuralist and discrete views of teaching, (2) American and British English as normative standards, (3) Taiwanese English as an inferior variety, and (4) native English speakers as insensitive interlocutors. The study highlights how digital ELT platforms may reproduce and intensify traditional Standard English ideologies in contemporary media environments.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Scientific Publishing
abstract: Artificial intelligence is now embedded across the scientific research and publishing ecosystem, influencing discovery, analysis, knowledge translation, authorship, peer review, and editorial workflows. In cardiovascular and biomedical sciences, these developments offer substantial opportunities to accelerate knowledge generation, integrate complex datasets, and improve efficiency and consistency. At the same time, they introduce new risks related to bias, transparency, data integrity, and authorship responsibility, potentially endangering trust in the scientific record. This commentary examines the evolving role of AI in biomedical publishing, with particular attention to generative models and machine learning tools. We review both benefits and limitations, highlight risks such as fabricated content, biased outputs, and erosion of accountability, and discuss why traditional detection approaches are insufficient. Instead, we argue for a shift toward transparency, provenance, and enforceable human responsibility as the core principles guiding AI use, ensuring that AI strengthens rather than undermines scientific rigour and public trust. We outline practical expectations for authors, reviewers, editors, and publishers, with emphasis on reporting standards, reproducibility under rapidly evolving model versions, and the conflict-of-interest implications of AI tooling for the editorial process itself.

title: From Learning Aid to Learning Escape: The Commodification of AI-Powered Educational Technologies and Their Impact on Chinese International Students' Cognitive and Ethical Development
abstract: This study critically investigates the engagement of Chinese international students towards AI-driven educational technologies, which are now strategically promoted in social media platforms such as Douyin (TikTok China) as easy access to graduation. Drawing from the interviews of 25 students and content analysis of 40 high-engagement ads, the findings reveal that AI tools such as wearable translators and tutoring apps do not merely provide academic aids but they are culturally marketed, emotionally framed, and ethically normalized especially within China's digital ecosystem. This phenomenon has paved way for students to experience cognitive offloading, moral disengagement, and intercultural disconnection, where the concept of “effortless learning” is eagerly propagated against the needed skills of critical thinking and academic integrity. Theories such as postdigital pedagogy, moral disengagement theory, and media dependency theory were evaluated and integrated to determine how the student expectations are shaped by algorithmic influences even before they set forth entering an international classroom. This present research hence, call for appropriate actions from the academe and policy makers to facilitate reforms in AI education and literacy as well as to create a more culturally-referenced and human-centered approaches to AI adoption and use. By identifying how students make use of digital tools before entering an international degree program, this will allow universities and relevant stakeholders to consider AI adoption not just a technological trend but a cultural phenomenon that needs to be further regulated and monitored.

title: Artificial intelligence in health professions education publishing: A content analysis of journal and publisher guidance
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being widely used by authors, reviewers and editors in the academic publishing process. However, there remains ambiguity about the boundaries of AI use. Amid this growing uncertainty, editors and publishers face an ongoing tension between a desire to advance the academic publishing process and a need to uphold scientific integrity. This study examined advisory and guideline statements about AI use by health professions education (HPE) journals. METHODS: We collected a corpus of texts relating to the use of AI in HPE journals from 22 HPE journals, 6 respective publishers and the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) policies in January 2026 relating to the use of AI in academic publishing. The corpus was examined using content analysis. RESULTS: Five main themes were identified from the analysis: 1) Accountable governance, 2) Protection of ethical standards, 3) Safeguarding of research integrity, 4) Maintenance of human oversight, and 5) Balancing of opportunities and risk. DISCUSSION: Overall, HPE journals predominantly frame the use of AI in academic publishing as a risk rather than an opportunity, with the overarching concern being a potential compromise of scientific integrity. Editors need to manage various tensions related to AI use and disclosure, including ensuring that policies keep up with the speed of technological advancement, and potentially broader impacts on the scholarly HPE field. As guidance on AI use continues to evolve, authors, reviewers and editors must ensure that they actively maintain and optimise their policies and practices in response to emerging evidence, including of unintended consequences.

title: Confronting Cancer’s Tradition: Redefinition and Resistance in Hope Formation among Wives of Men with Cancer in Iran
abstract: Background: Hope is a vital psychological resource that enables caregivers to endure and adapt to the challenges of a serious illness. In a broader qualitative study on hope formation among wives of men with cancer, several intrapersonal and extra-personal foundations were identified. This paper focuses on two key intrapersonal processes — Redefining Cancer and Rising against and Coping with it — to examine their internal dynamics more deeply. Objectives: The objective of this study was to explore how the two intrapersonal processes of redefining cancer and rising against and coping with it enable wives of men with cancer to reconstruct hope and reclaim a sense of agency within their caregiving role. Methods: A qualitative design guided by conventional content analysis was employed. Eleven wives of men with cancer (aged 29 - 55) were purposively recruited, and data saturation was reached after the 11th in-depth, semi-structured interview. Data were analyzed using Graneheim and Lundman’s five-step framework, generating 988 initial codes. Of these, 54 were clustered under two primary categories that form the analytical focus of this article. Results: Two key intrapersonal processes underlying hope formation emerged: (1) Redefining cancer and its aspects, involving the perception of the “cancer tradition” as both a destructive force and a potential catalyst for growth; and (2) rising against and coping, encompassing recognition of crisis, mobilization of agency, and reliance on goals and self-directed learning. Conclusions: This study demonstrates how caregiving spouses reconstruct hope and reclaim agency by redefining cancer and rising against its “tradition” as an oppressive cultural order. It introduces two novel intrapersonal cycles that link metaphor, meaning, and agency in the formation of hope, thereby offering a culturally sensitive conceptual lens for psycho-oncological supports and counseling practice with wives of men with cancer.
venue: Iranian Journal of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences

title: Mapping a Decade of AI-Generated Content in Digital Marketing: A Bibliometric Analysis (2016-2025)
abstract: Artificial-intelligence-generated content (AIGC), the autonomous production of text, images, audio and video by generative models, has rapidly become a central concern for digital-marketing scholarship and practice. This study maps the intellectual structure and evolution of research at the AIGC–digital-marketing intersection. Following PRISMA guidelines, 1400 Scopus-indexed articles and reviews published between 2016 and 2025 were retrieved and analysed in Bibliometrix and VOSviewer, combining performance analysis with science mapping. Annual output grew at a compound rate of 54.15% per year across three phases: a nascent period (2016–2019), gradual exploration (2020–2022) and explosive growth after late 2022, with 2025 alone contributing 52.6% of the corpus. Production is anchored by a United States–China dual core, with India acting as a bridging node. Co-citation and keyword analyses reveal a knowledge base that fuses established technology-adoption theories and structural-equation methodology with recent generative-AI manifestos, organised around four themes: content production, distribution channels, audience reach and responsible governance. Tool-level analysis shows that the literature is overwhelmingly text-centric (ChatGPT and the GPT family), while image and video generators and Asian social platforms remain under-examined. The study offers, to the best of our knowledge, one of the first decade-scale maps of this field, together with a structured agenda for future research.
venue: International Review of Management and Marketing

title: Trust, Attribution, and Adoption: Creator Perspectives on AI Disclosure and Provenance
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in visual content creation, including ideation, reference work, image generation, editing, and refinement. As AI becomes embedded in creative workflows, disclosure and provenance mechanisms are being introduced to communicate whetherand how AI was involved in the production of digital media. However, much existing research focuses on audience responses to AI disclosure, while less is known about how creators themselves understand disclosure decisions, interpret provenance information, and evaluate adoption conditions in their own work.This study investigates how visual content creators perceive AI-use disclosure and provenance mechanisms, using Content Credentials (C2PA) as a concrete example. The purpose is to generate creator-centred insights and translate them into actionable UX requirements for disclosureand provenance systems. The study is based on qualitative semi-structured interviews with ten visual content creators, including students, early-career creators, professionals, and freelancers working with illustration, graphic design, UX/UI, branding, marketing, and related visual practices. Participants discussed their creative workflows, AI use, disclosure attitudes, interpretation of current AI labels, and responses to a screenshot-based walkthrough of Content Credentials.The analysis resulted in six themes. Participants did not treat AI use as a binary disclosure trigger, instead, disclosure thresholds depended on creative contribution, final output involvement, and perceived consequences. Disclosure was valued as transparency and honesty, but also seen as a risk to perceived skill, originality, pricing, and professional value. Decisions varied acrosspublic, client-facing, educational, workplace, and platform governed contexts. Generic AI labelswere often considered too broad because they failed to communicate the type, stage, or degreeof AI involvement. Content Credentials were viewed as potentially useful trust infrastructure, but fragile due to metadata loss, bypassability, incomplete records, limited platform support, and possible misunderstanding. Adoption depended on workflow integration, visibility, creator control, and privacy boundaries.The study contributes empirically grounded UX requirements for creator-centred AI disclosure and provenance design. These requirements emphasise stage-specific disclosure, clearer distinctions between AI assistance and AI generation, layered information, context-sensitive disclosure profiles, provenance persistence, limitation communication, and creator control over public process information.

title: The Disclosure-Detection Nexus in Generative AI: An Integrated Analysis of Ethical Implications in Academia
abstract: This article analyses the ethical challenges created by the growing use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, with particular focus on the tension between AI use disclosure and AI-generated content detection. Through a structured literature review and thematic analysis, it shows that current AI detection tools are unreliable, biased, and prone to false positives, often undermining academic trust and fairness. The study argues for a shift away from surveillance-driven detection toward a disclosure-led, trust-based approach in which transparent AI use supports academic integrity, while detection serves only as a limited, human-augmented safeguard. It offers practical recommendations for institutions, educators, and policymakers on disclosure policies, assessment redesign, AI literacy, and ethical governance, and outlines future research directions for responsible and sustainable GenAI integration in academia.

Causal Reality Attestation: A Conceptual Framework for Verifiable Physical Provenance of Digital Media
abstract: Causal Reality Attestation (CRA) is a conceptual framework for reasoning about whether a digital artifact was produced through a claimed physical interaction, rather than attempting to infer that history from the artifact alone. The paper distinguishes physical-event factuality—the historical question of whether the claimed causal relation actually occurred—from attested physical provenance, the evidence-relative support that a verifier can assign to that claim. It proposes a typed causal-evidence graph, a separate dependency model for shared compromise relations, and Minimum-Control Cost (MCC) as a dependency-sensitive measure of the least modeled control cost sufficient for forgery under an explicit adversary and calibration model. The paper does not claim a new multi-witness architecture, proof-of-location mechanism, or new mathematical optimization technique. Instead, it positions CRA as a conceptual and analytical framework that connects existing work in content provenance, hardware attestation, secure capture, proof-of-location, contextual witnessing, attack modeling, common-cause failure analysis, and related techniques. This is a position paper and research agenda, not a security proof, protocol standard, or empirical evaluation. AI use disclosure. title: ScholarScribe: A Privacy-First Local LLM Writing Companion for Researchers
abstract: ScholarScribe is a desktop application that supports researchers in the preparation of scholarly manuscripts through a suite of local, privacy-preserving tools. The application runs entirely on the user's device, requires no cloud-based application programming interfaces (APIs), collects no telemetry, and transmits no user-generated content to any external host. Drawing on contemporary research into the limitations of AI-generated text detectors (Liang et al., 2023; Weber-Wulff et al., 2023), ScholarScribe is explicitly designed not to facilitate the evasion of such detectors. Instead, it offers transparent, auditable tools for text cleaning, citation validation, document structure analysis, style analysis, AI-use disclosure generation, and structured abstract drafting—functions that align with established norms of research integrity. The application is built on the Tauri 2 framework (Rust backend, Svelte frontend) and uses Ollama as its local large language model (LLM) runtime, enabling the use of open-weight models such as Google's Gemma 3, Alibaba's Qwen 3, Microsoft's Phi-4, DeepSeek R1, and Meta's Llama 3.3 without reliance on proprietary inference services.

title: Relational Reversibility: Structural Conditions for Recovery Capacity Generation in Adaptive Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: RT4 studies how interaction changes a declared system's ability to recover after disruption. It distinguishes recovery supplied by current support from capacity retained after earlier cooperative learning or repair, and separates autonomous, assisted, and preparation effects. Support paths and failure-transmission paths are treated as different objects. An exact finite-cascade benchmark isolates support loss, transmission removal, and the task cost of hub removal. A trust-connectivity score remains a candidate predictor rather than a general recovery probability. Unreproducible demonstrations and an undocumented collaboration analysis are retired; causal capacity-generation mechanisms and incremental predictive value require direct experiments. abstract: This paper develops an audit specification for separately controlling participation, signal gain, timing, information exposure, and permission in multi-agent workflows. Dynamic Influence Balance names the candidate architecture. title: AI-Augmented Research Without Replacing Evidence: A Methodological Framework for MIND Plus
abstract: This working paper presents the methodological principles of MIND Plus, an independent research and publishing project that uses artificial intelligence to expand the scale of scholarly discovery, comparison, synthesis and question generation without delegating scientific authority to AI systems. The framework treats generative AI as an analytical instrument operating inside a traceable evidence architecture. Claims are expected to remain connected to identifiable sources; disagreement and uncertainty are preserved rather than edited away; and final responsibility for research direction, interpretation and publication remains human. The paper describes a workflow that combines open scholarly infrastructures, citation mapping, structured comparison, verification and critical analysis. It also defines limits for AI use, including the risks of hallucination, automation bias, conceptual flattening and false comparability. The central proposal is that AI can increase the breadth and speed of research only when amplification is paired with explicit epistemic controls. title: Motor Fatigue Degradation Monitoring: An implementable specification for adaptive timing in switch and dwell access
abstract: Access timings for switch scanning and dwell selection are configured once and then held fixed, while motor fatigue changes the user within the session: latency rises, accuracy falls, and the interface does not move. This note specifies Motor Fatigue Degradation (MFD) monitoring, a rolling-window analysis of interaction latency and target accuracy that detects within-session decline and recommends either an extended timing multiplier or a break. The specification is complete enough to implement independently: inputs, windowing, baseline selection, the adaptation rule, break logic, and all seven parameters with defaults. It states plainly that the parameter values are engineering choices rather than findings, documents the deliberate decision that the multiplier only ratchets upward, and sets out the failure modes, including that fatigue and disengagement are not distinguishable by this method. No efficacy claim is made and no trial has been conducted. The evaluation the method requires is described so that a team with access to switch and dwell users can run it. title: Residual Causal Information After Complete Decomposition: Multi-Channel Constraints and Simple Structure Recovery
abstract: This preprint examines whether complete decomposition necessarily eliminates every recoverable physical constraint about a prior organism, or whether distributed residues and environmental modifications can preserve measurable retrodictive information across distinct physical channels. It distinguishes destruction of the original carrier from total causal-information loss, separates practical from principled failure, and frames the problem using conditional residue distributions. Next scientific experiment: Cellulase-based paper degradation will be used as a simplified, controlled analogue of enzyme-mediated material breakdown in natural decomposition. The comparison is limited to this general mechanism; the enzymes, substrates, reaction networks, and biological conditions differ, so the experiment should not be interpreted as a complete model of natural decomposition. Managing Design Interfaces in Utility-Scale Solar PV and High-Voltage Substation Projects in Saudi Arabia
abstract: Utility-scale solar photovoltaic projects connected through high-voltage substations depend on the successful integration of many technical, organizational and contractual interfaces. In Saudi Arabia, fast-track delivery and the involvement of developers, project companies, consultants, EPC contractors, grid stakeholders and equipment vendors increase the consequences of unclear design ownership, provisional information and delayed decisions. This paper presents a practical governance approach for managing design interfaces in Saudi solar PV and high-voltage substation projects. It combines a focused review of interface management, project integration, design development and Saudi construction-project literature with anonymized observations from professional practice. The paper identifies practical controls including clear responsibility allocation, interface registers, information-readiness checks, decision tracking, assumption management, configuration control, escalation and evidence-based closure. It does not claim measured performance improvements; its contribution is a structured operating approach that can be applied and further evaluated on future renewable-energy projects. Label “Buatan AI” pada Iklan TikTok untuk Produk Hedonik: Peran Pengetahuan Persuasi (Konseptual vs. Sikap) terhadap Sikap terhadap Iklan
abstract: The adoption of AI auto-labeling by TikTok since 2024 has established transparency in AI use as a new standard in digital advertising; however, its impact on consumer responses, particularly for hedonic products that are sensitive to warmth and authenticity, remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM), this study distinguishes ad-specific persuasion knowledge (PK) into a conceptual dimension (recognition of content as advertising) and an attitudinal dimension (skepticism toward persuasive motives), and examines how the “AI-generated” label influences both dimensions and, in turn, attitude toward the ad (Aad). Using a between-subjects experimental design with a sample of 387 Indonesian TikTok users aged 18–35 years, this research manipulated the presence of an AI label on TikTok ads for a hedonic product (premium snacks). Data were analyzed using path analysis with PLS-SEM. The results show that the AI label significantly increases conceptual PK (β = .487, p < .001) and attitudinal PK (β = .312, p < .001), while conceptual PK in turn strengthens attitudinal PK (β = .394, p < .001). Attitudinal PK subsequently reduces Aad significantly (β = –.618, p < .001). Serial mediation analysis confirms the pathway AI label → conceptual PK → attitudinal PK → Aad (β = –.118, 95% CI [–.172, –.066]) with full mediation (total effect β = –.391). These findings provide three main contributions: (1) formalizing the separation of cognitive (conceptual PK) and affective (attitudinal PK) effects of AI-use disclosure; (2) demonstrating a trade-off between AI transparency and the advertising effectiveness of hedonic products in short-form video contexts; and (3) offering practical implications for TikTok advertisers in the form of content humanization strategies (human-in-the-loop narratives, warmth cues) and label format design (placement at the beginning of the video, semi-transparent display) to preserve affective effectiveness while remaining ethical and transparent. The study concludes that AI transparency, although normative and increasingly unavoidable, entails persuasive costs that need to be mitigated through warm and authentic creative design.

title: Conscious Cost and God: The Un-foreclosable Addressee
abstract: This paper works from below — from a social ontology of cost, recognition, and foreclosure, rather than from the limits of language or being — toward one function of the concept of God, and arrives at a single functional claim: before a rule, the certificate of an answer’s sufficiency is always the answerer’s to issue; before an addressee it never is — so the office of keeping a question open belongs to an addressee, not a rule. Treated functionally, with the questions of God’s existence, nature, and intent set aside, God occupies not the position of the answer that closes the question whom does this serve? but that of the un-foreclosable addressee whose standing keeps it open. The argument extends the Conscious Cost account — developed in earlier work for interpersonal relations, commons, markets, and democratic polities — to its highest name, using the same apparatus: the gap between the cost an arrangement exacts and the cost it is granted (Cq, Cs), the reach of concern (R), voluntariness (V), tacitness (T), and the independence of self-worth (P). The account claims one facet, not a description of God; it situates itself against the apophatic tradition — the via negativa, Tillich, Marion, Caputo — and locates its difference in derivation, not doctrine. The program from which the account derives began in autoethnographic observation rather than a literature-first survey; the present paper extends its apparatus by structural analysis. Keywords: Conscious Cost; foreclosure; the un-foreclosable addressee; functional account of God; apophatic theology (via negativa); social ontology; autoethnography AI-Use Disclosure The author conceived and developed the theory and its argument and directed all substantive content. AI assistance with scientific writing: Possibilities, pitfalls, and ethical considerations
abstract: Scientific writing is critical to performing research, requiring careful attention to detail, clarity of expression, and adherence to established standards. While the importance of good scientific writing cannot be overstated, it is often a challenging and time-consuming process. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to help streamline and improve scientific writing. By leveraging machine learning and natural language processing algorithms, AI assistance has the potential to enhance the quality and efficiency of scientific writing.

title: Measuring Temporal Envelopes Shared by Geometric Transformations: Recurring Structure Across Multiple Video Collections and the Limits of Cross-Work Prediction
abstract: This preprint has not been peer reviewed. The manuscript is in Japanese; this description summarizes the corrected version in English. Motion graphics combine translation, rotation, and scale, whose units differ. This study represents the distribution of each channel’s frame-to-frame change over relative time within a cut as a unit-sum temporal envelope. In 886 eligible cuts from a fourth video collection fixed before content inspection, within-cut cosine similarity exceeded duration-matched between-cut controls for translation–rotation (+0.164), translation–scale (+0.148), and rotation–scale (+0.164). None of 10,000 permutations reached the observed differences. These three geometric channels, derived from the same partial-affine estimation, showed recurring descriptive temporal structure; the result does not establish a universal rule or independent sensing of the channels. Version 2 corrects the description of the measurement used for the additional analysis. Version 1 called the appearance channel a Shannon entropy difference, but the implementation and saved data used the pixel residual after geometric alignment. Subsequent synthetic calibration showed that this residual can also pick up geometric motion. The numerical results are unchanged: alignment with the residual was 0.792 versus a permutation-control median of 0.687 (difference 0.105), and adding the geometric envelope reduced cross-work prediction mean squared error by 3.45%, with improvement in 8 of 11 works, below the prespecified 9-of-11 criterion. These statistics cannot establish coordination with independent appearance change, so that interpretation is withheld. No new entropy analysis is included. The paper’s central claim is limited to the temporal-envelope comparison among the three geometric channels. The package contains the corrected Japanese manuscript, figures, claim-to-evidence and revision audits, checksums, and supporting results. title: Applying an Agentic Coding Tool for Improving Published Algorithm Implementations
abstract: We present a two-stage pipeline for AI-assisted improvement of published algorithm implementations. In the first stage, a large language model with research capabilities identifies recently published algorithms satisfying explicit experimental criteria. In the second stage, Claude Code is given a prompt to reproduce the reported baseline and then iterate an improvement process. We apply this pipeline to published algorithm implementations spanning multiple research domains. Claude Code reported that all eleven experiments yielded improvements. Each improvement could be achieved within a single working day. We analyse the human contributions that remain indispensable, including selecting the target, verifying experimental validity, assessing novelty and impact, providing computational resources, and writing with appropriate AI-use disclosure. Finally, we discuss implications for peer review and academic publishing.

title: Cultivating Critical AI Literacy in an ESL Academic Writing Classroom: A Reflective Inquiry
abstract: With the rapid rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI literacy has become a critical issue in higher education, shifting the focus from basic use to ethical and critical engagement. Drawing on the AI literacy framework (Warschauer et al., 2023) and the critical APSE model (Wang & Wang, 2025), this practitioner-inquiry examines classroom practices designed to foster critical AI literacy in an English as a Second Language (ESL) academic writing course. The findings reveal three key instructional practices that contribute to the development of critical AI literacy: (1) developing prompt literacy, (2) critically evaluating AI-generated outputs by composing counter-text, and (3) drafting AI use disclosure statements. These findings highlight pedagogical approaches that support students’ ethical, reflective, and critical engagement with AI tools in academic writing contexts.

title: Cross-Cell Consistency as a Supportive Validation Signal: A Subject-Level Case Study in the DFG Cell-Card Protocol
abstract: This record contains Document 07 of the DFG Empirical Programme submission package: Cross-Cell Consistency as a Supportive Validation Signal: A Subject-Level Case Study in the DFG Cell-Card Protocol. This short technical note documents a cross-cell consistency observation from the DFG Empirical Programme. The same biological subject, DANDI:001611 sub-25273, appears as the shared high-end anomaly in two independent cell-level operationalisations: H1-η cascade-exponent fitting under the canonical Beggs-Plenz avalanche protocol, and H5-γ Jacobian-spectral-radius recovery analysis. The note argues that this agreement is a supportive validation signal for the cell-card operationalisation protocol, not a stand-alone validation of either cell. H1-η remains Joint-Incompatible at the cell level, while H5-γ remains Compatible at session-level aggregation with subject-level caveats. The cross-cell observation instead supports the idea that independent operationalisations can sometimes identify a shared substrate-state property. The note proposes adding a Cross-Cell Consistency framework to Paper A: when two or more cells share a substrate dataset, their subject-level outputs should be compared. Consistent subject ordering across independent operationalisations may serve as supportive cross-cell consistency evidence, but it does not propagate compatibility across cells. This record is part of the DFG Empirical Programme submission package. It assumes the regime-atlas methodology established in Document 01, the Compatibility Atlas v1.3. Cell-level incompatibility should be interpreted as a regime-boundary marker rather than theory-level falsification. AI use disclosure. title: Shared Peak Time Bands of Geometric Transformations in Finished Videos: Within-Cut Recurrence and the Limits of Between-Cut Transitions
abstract: This preprint has not been peer reviewed. The manuscript is in Japanese. Motion graphics combine translation, rotation, and scale within a cut. This study asks whether completed videos contain recurring peak orders, shared peak time bands, or between-cut transition patterns among these geometric transformations. Frame-to-frame translation (T), rotation (R), and scale (S) changes were summarized in ten relative-time bins, and bins attaining the maximum were treated as peak bands. No consistent transformation order exceeded the matched permutation control. In contrast, rotation and scale shared a peak band more often than controls that preserved work identity and approximate cut duration while breaking within-cut correspondence. In a validation set fixed by publicly credited production source, 634 cuts from eight non-overlapping production-source labels yielded an observed overlap rate of 0.319 versus 0.161 under the control (difference 0.157; p=0.00010); all eight sources showed an observed value above the control. Replacing bin means with medians preserved the result (difference 0.165). No candidate rule was found for transitions among adjacent cuts. The recurring structure supported here is therefore within-cut sharing of a coarse peak time band, not a fixed transformation sequence or a between-cut progression. The study does not establish frame-level synchrony, production settings, author intent, perceptual pleasantness, or a universal rule across authors. abstract: Z0 — Umbrella Pre-Registration: UHA Space-Frame, Coordinate Provenance, and Ωm Baseline Research Program (v1.2-hybrid, bootstrap commit d842691). Three-track research program testing whether the Universal Horizon Address (UHA) coordinate framework and EB carrier uncertainty propagation can: (1) operate as an overlay layer for space-operations coordinate handling (Track 0); (2) improve cross-survey cosmological consistency through better coordinate provenance (Track A); (3) reduce apparent cosmological tensions by unifying Ωm baselines across surveys (Track B). This umbrella does not run any analysis itself. It locks the program structure, the non-claims, the termination criteria (kill switches), and the deposit chain so that subsequent per-track pre-registrations (Z1, Z2, Z3) inherit a consistent framework and so that post-hoc rescue of any failed branch is structurally impossible. Locked components: H0/H1 hypotheses for Track A and Track B; baseline / improvement / primary-success / AgreementMetric / TensionMetric definitions; data-handling rules (outlier, missing-data, FDR); formula-level operational model locks; evidence-class thresholds (Exceptional / Strong / Moderate / Null); 18 primary kill switches (KS1-9, K0-8) plus four cross-track cascade rules; always-active circuit-breakers (deposit-DOI-before-compute, marketing-language audit); two-stage failure-publication commitment (Stage 1 within 14 days, Stage 2 when packaging complete). §7 Kill-switch interpretation preamble (author-locked): kill switches are auditable decision rules, not descriptive guidelines; each switch satisfies three structural conditions (observable trigger, defined action, traceable effect); under ambiguity, conservative interpretation applies (halt or downgrade rather than extend or reinterpret the claim); the switch count reflects coverage across independent failure modes, not unwarranted precision.
