title: Timing of AI Disclosure in Promotional Video Advertising : An Experimental Study of Consumer Trust, Attitude and Scepticism
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into advertising production, questions surrounding transparency and consumer responses to AI disclosure have become more important. Prior research shows that AI disclosure can influence advertising evaluations, but existing studies have mainly examined disclosure as a present-or-absent condition, often in static advertising formats. Less attention has been given to whether the timing of disclosure matters, particularly in promotional video advertising where the message unfolds sequentially over time. This study examines how the timing of AI disclosure influences consumers’ trust, attitude and scepticism towards AI-generated promotional video content. Drawing on disclosure timing research, with the Persuasion Knowledge Model used as a supporting theoretical framework, the study compares three experimental conditions: no disclosure, pre-exposure disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 239 participants, who were exposed to one version of an AI-generated promotional video before completing a structured questionnaire. The findings did not reveal statistically significant differences between the disclosure conditions for trust, attitude or scepticism. However, the descriptive results followed a consistent directional pattern, with pre-exposure disclosure associated with slightly lower trust and attitude and slightly higher scepticism than both no disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. Exploratory analyses further suggested that participants’ familiarity with generative AI and their broader attitudes towards AI-generated video content may be relevant contextual factors influencing consumer evaluations. The study contributes to AI disclosure research by conceptualising disclosure as a temporally positioned cue within promotional video advertising. It suggests that disclosure timing may be theoretically meaningful, but that timing alone may be insufficient to produce strong immediate effects on consumer evaluation.
venue: Linnéuniversitetet, Institutionen för marknadsföring och turismvetenskap (MTS)

title: Artificial Intelligence Contribution Index (ACI): A Lightweight Framework for Declaring LLM Contributions to Human-Authored Documents
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how documents and other intellectual artifacts are conceived, structured, and expressed. However, norms about human-AI collaboration, and therefore in particular for declaring AI involvement in human-authored work, remain inconsistent: some institutions discourage any use, while others require only generic disclosure statements that fail to specify the nature and extent of AI contribution. This article proposes the Artificial Intelligence Contribution Index (ACI), a lightweight framework for transparent disclosure of AI assistance in authorship. ACI distinguishes between two independent dimensions of contribution – content and form – and assigns each a four-level scale, from no AI involvement to substantial AI-driven production. Conceptually, the framework is grounded in the rhetorical stages of inventio, dispositio, and elocutio, which together provide a structured account of how meaning is generated, organized, and articulated. On this basis, ACI captures whether AI contributed primarily to idea generation and conceptual organization, linguistic and stylistic expression, or both. The framework is designed to support explicit attribution rather than post-hoc detection, thereby emphasizing authorial responsibility over surveillance-based approaches. By offering a simple, modular, and interoperable attribution schema, ACI aims to strengthen transparency, accountability, and trust in human-AI co-creation across scholarly, educational and professional domains. Keywords Generative artificial intelligence; authorship; disclosure; transparency; accountability; human–AI collaboration.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Capabilities in Sustainability Reporting of Oil and Gas Companies
abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI)-specifically large language models (LLMs) enhanced by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technology-can be applied across the sustainability reporting cycle of oil and gas companies. Drawing on recent empirical research and the evolving Russian regulatory framework, including the 2023 Methodological Recommendations on Sustainability Reporting and the 2025 Business Social Capital Standard, the study identifies three functional stages at which generative AI offers distinct capabilities: primary data processing, analytical elaboration, and final disclosure drafting. For each stage, specific accounting and methodological conditions are proposed to govern AI deployment responsibly. The paper argues that realising the potential of generative AI in sustainability reporting requires not merely technological adoption but deliberate adaptation of accounting policies, prompt governance, and expert oversight mechanisms. The findings are particularly relevant for Russian energy companies operating within a rapidly developing national sustainability disclosure regime.

title: Towards Responsible Generative AI Use in EU R&I Grants: A Self-Assessment Model and the path to a Governance Framework
abstract: This paper explores the transformative impact of Generative AI on EU Research and Innovation (R&I) grant preparation processes. It introduces a Self-Assessment Model aimed at promoting responsible AI use while paving the way for a Governance Framework. Drawing on insights from recent surveys and guidelines, the study analyzes the widespread adoption of Generative AI tools, highlighting their benefits and challenges. With 70% of surveyed stakeholders already utilizing these tools, issues such as transparency, accountability, originality, and institutional guidance are brought to the forefront. The paper seeks to address the current lack of standardized mechanisms for AI disclosure, proposing actionable strategies to safeguard research integrity without hindering innovation.

title: Generative AI Needs Adaptive Governance
abstract: Because of the speed of its development, broad scope of application, and its ability to augment human performance, generative AI challenges the very notions of governance, trust, and human agency. The technology's capacity to mimic human knowledge work, feedback loops including significant uptick in users, research, investor, policy, and media attention, data and compute resources, all lead to rapidly increasing capabilities. For those reasons, adaptive governance, where AI governance and AI co-evolve, is essential for governing generative AI. In sharp contrast to traditional governance's regulatory regimes that are based on a mix of rigid one-and-done provisions for disclosure, registration and risk management, which in the case of AI carry the potential for regulatory misalignment, this paper argues that generative AI calls for adaptive governance. We define adaptive governance in the context of AI and outline an adaptive AI governance framework. We outline actors, roles, as well as both shared and actors-specific policy activities. We further provide examples of how the framework could be operationalized in practice. We then explain that the adaptive AI governance stance is not without its risks and limitations, such as insufficient oversight, insufficient depth, regulatory uncertainty, and regulatory capture, and provide potential approaches to fix these shortcomings.

title: From Detection to Trust: Managing Cybersecurity Risks of Generative AI Systems in Organizations
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems in organizational environments introduces new and complex challenges in the field of information assurance and cybersecurity. While generative AI technologies, including large language models, provide significant benefits in automation, decision support, and knowledge management, they also create emerging risk vectors related to data confidentiality, integrity, system misuse, and regulatory compliance. This paper aims to examine cybersecurity risks associated with generative AI systems from an organizational perspective, with a particular focus on trust, governance, and cybersecurity risk management. The study is based on a structured review of recent academic literature, industry reports, and regulatory frameworks addressing AI security and information assurance. Key threat categories are identified, including prompt injection attacks, unauthorized data disclosure, model manipulation, lack of transparency, and limited auditability of AI-driven systems. The analysis highlights how these risks affect organizational decision-making, accountability, and compliance with data protection regulations. Based on the findings, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for managing cybersecurity risks of generative AI systems that integrates technical safeguards, organizational policies, and compliance mechanisms. The framework emphasizes the transition from reactive detection toward trust-oriented governance and continuous risk monitoring. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions focused on empirical validation of generative AI security controls and their effectiveness in strengthening organizational information assurance.

title: AI as Aladdin's Lamp: From Generative Media to Wish-Responsive Worlds
abstract: When you type a prompt into a generative AI system and a story, an image, a video, or a virtual environment appears in response, you are doing something different from reading, looking, or stepping into a world. You are summoning one. This paper argues that generative artificial intelligence is not just a fourth medium of world-disclosure alongside fiction, painting, and immersive technology. It is an integrative engine that operates across all three previous continua at once, and it adds a structurally new operation: wish-responsiveness. The user articulates a desire; the medium summons a world in response. This paper, the fourth and final in a four-part programme on world-making media, completes the disclosure-theoretic framework developed across the earlier papers. It shows that generative AI can occupy any of the five modes—preservation, reconstruction, transformation, suspension, dissolution—within the narrative, pictorial, and immersive registers, often within a single artifact. It identifies wish-responsiveness as a medium-specific parameter with three sub-elements: articulation fidelity, summoning latency, and recursive responsiveness. And it argues, drawing on prior work, that the worlds generative AI summons remain ontologically grounded in physical reality even when their experiential vividness rivals lived inhabitation. The Aladdin’s Lamp metaphor is not decorative. The lamp captures three structural features no other metaphor captures together: wish-articulation as the activating operation, summoning rather than constructing, and power without ontological autonomy. The lamp also carries its own caution: wishes can be misformulated, the response can over-deliver in ways the wisher did not intend, and the wish-responsive medium can become a substitute for the agency it was meant to amplify. The paper engages contemporary philosophy of AI (Floridi, Coeckelbergh, Smith, Bender et al., Chiang, Shanahan, Cappelen and Dever), the philosophy of technology (Heidegger, Stiegler, Hui), critical AI studies (Crawford, Noble, Haraway), AI aesthetics (Manovich), the extended-mind tradition (Clark), and Benjamin’s foundational essay on technology and aura. It concludes by naming the unified theoretical framework the four papers together produce—the disclosure-theoretic ontology of media, or the graded modal disclosure framework—and offering it as an analytic tool for future scholarship on world-making media.

title: Augmented inventorship: rethinking patent law in the age of generative AI
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now participates in tasks constitutive of invention—problem framing, hypothesis generation, and design—yet patent doctrine remains anchored to a natural-person rule that offers limited guidance for AI-intensive workflows. This Article advances augmented inventorship, a conservative but operationally modern attribution doctrine that preserves human inventorship while making AI’s generative role legible and auditable at the moment of conception. Drawing on an analogy to augmented immunology, the framework identifies two design criteria—directability (independent and substantive human intellectual judgment steering model behavior or selection) and traceability (a reviewable, claim-centered record linking human reasons to claim elements)—and translates them into a proportionate evidentiary practice: a Computational Traceability Report and a Human–Machine Contribution Statement. These instruments are content-rich but code-light. They support enablement and sufficiency, clarify claim drafting and construction, reduce prosecution and litigation error costs, and balance evidentiary transparency with trade-secret sensitivity through proportional disclosure. Situated within—and distinguished from—the growing literature on AI inventorship and disclosure, the doctrine aligns with existing law (US conception and significant-contribution standards; the UK’s ‘actual deviser’; EPC sufficiency) and is compatible with TRIPS disclosure norms. Rather than demanding ‘more disclosure’ in the abstract, augmented inventorship supplies an administrable grammar for human accountability in AI-assisted research.

title: TRANSPARENT TECHNOLOGY: EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF AI-GENERATED AD DISCLOSURE ON CONSUMER TRUST, AUTHENTICITY, AND PURCHASE INTENTION
abstract: This study investigates how disclosure of AI-generated advertising content influences consumer perceptions and behaviors in an increasingly AI-driven marketing landscape. Using a 2×2 experimental design that manipulates AI-generative ad disclosure (present versus absent) and beliefs about AI's capability (high versus low complexity tasks), we examine the effects on perceived authenticity, trust, and purchase intention. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework, we theorize that disclosure serves as a critical stimulus affecting internal evaluative processes and subsequent consumer responses. Findings may reveal that disclosure effects are significantly moderated by consumers' pre-existing beliefs about AI's capabilities to perform complex tasks. This research examines the impact of AI-generated ad disclosure, focusing on ad content creation, consumers' perceptions of trust and authenticity, and the subsequent effect on consumers' purchase intention. This study contributes to the AI advertising body of literature by investigating how consumers respond differently to AI-generated ad content disclosure. As these technologies become more widespread in advertising, understanding how AI disclosure affects consumer perceptions of authenticity, trust, and purchase intentions becomes essential for advertisers and policymakers to develop appropriate disclosure guidelines.
venue: Global Alliance of Marketing and Management Associations

title: The Showdown Effect: A Double-Blind Epistemic Isolation (DBEI) Framework for Assessing Generative AI's Reverse-Engineering Capability Boundary
abstract: This preprint proposes the Double-Blind Epistemic Isolation (DBEI) framework to assess whether generative AI can reconstruct the core architecture of an unpublished, multi-domain complex engineering system using only publicly available prior art. Under epistemic isolation, the AI consistently failed to cross the nonlinear coupling boundaries of the target system; upon disclosure of the complete information at the "showdown trigger," its analytical focus shifted from challenging physical feasibility to scrutinizing procedural and disclosure formalities. All experimental transcripts are sealed with SHA-256 and a Merkle Tree (MerkleRoot independently reproducible), ensuring tamper-evidence. This is a single-target, single-rater proof of concept; broader claims await multi-target, multi-model, and multi-rater validation.

title: Continuous Temporal Auditing of AI Training Data Disclosure: A Cryptographically Anchored Observational Framework at Ecosystem Scale
abstract: We present CROVIA, a continuously operating observational system for monitoring training data disclosure practices across the AI model ecosystem. Our system operates at ecosystem scale, monitoring 4,843 models from 1,152 organizations with automated daily observation cycles anchored to a cryptographic Merkle chain now at height 5,480. Analysis reveals that 57.6% exhibit CRITICAL disclosure gaps and the ecosystem-wide average compliance score is 26.8% across 20 disclosure elements mapped to 11 regulatory jurisdictions including the EU AI Act, GDPR, CCPA, and China's Generative AI Provisions. We introduce the Temporal Proof of Absence (TPA) — a cryptographically verifiable artifact asserting that specific disclosure elements were absent from a model's public documentation at a specific point in time, deployed across 200 models with full proof chains including Pedersen commitments on secp256k1, Ed25519 signatures, and temporal pressure scoring. Live registry: https://registry.croviatrust.com

title: Responsible Disclosure in the Age of Generative AI: A Normative Model for Dual-Use Risk
abstract: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as large language models (LLMs) has created a profound disclosure dilemma: when should potentially dangerous models or findings be shared openly, withheld, or released in a controlled manner? Traditional norms of open science and open source software emphasize transparency, reproducibility, and collective progress, yet the dual-use nature of frontier LLMs raises unprecedented challenges. Unrestricted disclosure can enable malicious use cases such as cyberattacks, automated disinformation campaigns, large-scale fraud, or even synthetic biology misuse. In contrast, excessive secrecy risks undermining trust, slowing scientific progress, and concentrating power in a small number of actors. This paper develops a normative model for responsible disclosure that integrates utilitarian, deontological, and virtue-ethical reasoning to justify a proportional approach rather than binary openness or secrecy. We introduce a Disclosure Decision Matrix that evaluates four key dimensions: risk severity, exploitability, mitigation availability, and public benefit of transparency. It then recommends one of three courses of action: full release, staged or controlled release, or temporary restriction until safeguards mature. The contribution is twofold. First, it provides a principled ethical framework that links philosophical justification directly to operational disclosure practices, bridging the gap between theory and governance. Second, it translates this framework into actionable criteria that policymakers, research institutions, and developers can consistently apply across evolving AI systems. By combining ethical reasoning with practical decision tools, the findings underscore that responsible disclosure in AI is neither absolute secrecy nor unqualified openness but a dynamic, proportional strategy responsive to both technological advances and societal risks.
venue: Blue Eyes Intelligence Engineering and Sciences Engineering and Sciences Publication - BEIESP

title: Individual AI Use Maturity: A Practical Framework for Responsible AI Practice
abstract: This description outlines the Individual AI Use Maturity Framework (iAUMF), a five-stage conceptual model designed to assess and guide responsible AI use in daily life. While generative AI is deeply embedded in ordinary routines, a critical "oversight gap" persists where users benefit from fluent outputs but fail to verify accuracy or limitations. Drawing on trust in automation, automation bias, and cognitive offloading, the iAUMF structures human-AI interaction across seven crosscutting dimensions: purpose clarity, prompt strategy, verification rigor, epistemic independence, privacy protection, disclosure, and accountability.

title: How Firms Communicate Artificial Intelligence in Earnings Calls: Opportunities, Risks, and Market Reactions
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a prominent focus of corporate disclosures in earnings conference calls, yet informational value of such disclosures remains difficult for external stakeholders to evaluate. Rather than examining whether firms mention AI, this study investigates how firms communicate AI opportunities and risks. We develop a human-in-theloop generative AI framework integrating domain-specific dictionaries with LLM-based annotation to systematically analyze AI-related disclosures. We find that AI opportunity disclosures are positively associated with cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), driven primarily by AI exploitation opportunities, while competitive and operational AI risk disclosures are negatively associated with CAR. Over longer horizons, AI opportunity disclosures predict superior firm performance, while the negative relationship between AI risk disclosures and firm performance attenuates. Disclosure specificity and unscripted AI disclosure further moderate these relationships. This study shifts attention from AI adoption to strategic external communication, contributing to the literature on AI business value, fintech, and corporate disclosure.

title: Generative AI in Computer Engineering
abstract: This academic practice guide provides a curriculum-wide framework for the responsible use of generative artificial intelligence in Computer Engineering(CNG) education and research. It is written specifically for CNG students, teaching assistants, supervisors, lecturers, and academic programme teams who need practical guidance on using AI tools without compromising technical understanding, verification, academic integrity, or reproducibility. The document covers the use of generative AI across major Computer Engineering areas, including programming, algorithms, mathematics, digital logic, computer architecture, embedded systems, operating systems, databases, networks, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science, software engineering, capstone projects, thesis work, and technical communication. It emphasises that AI-generated outputs must be treated as candidate artefacts requiring validation through compilers, tests, simulations, synthesis tools, benchmarks, proof reconstruction, verified sources, and human engineering judgement. The guide also introduces responsible workflows, assessment considerations, disclosure practices, reproducibility expectations, thesis and research directions, prompt templates, and the ACCEPT framework for accountable AI use in CNG academic contexts.

title: Greenwashing Governance through ESG Disclosure: A Double Face for Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in producing, interpreting, and verifying information on the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) information. Companies are under increasing pressure to report on ESG information that is extensive, useful, credible, comparable, and decision-useful. However, the proliferation of ESG disclosure does not guarantee more transparency. Rather, it has increased the risk of symbolic disclosure, narrative inflation, and greenwashing. In this context, AI is emerging as an attractive governance technology but also as a new source for reporting risk. In this narrative review, we discuss how AI could influence ESG disclosure quality, or even the governance of greenwashing. Here, we argue that we need to understand AI beyond its use as a technological solution to process sustainability information, but also as a socio-technical form of governance that transforms the production, evaluation, and contestation of sustainability claims. Drawing from the literature on ESG disclosure, greenwashing, computational text analysis, sustainability reporting and ESG assurance, our contribution is to develop a three-level framework in which AI can be used both as a disclosure mechanism and as an audit instrument, with the potential of also promoting indirect normative behavior. The work presented here builds on this triple role of AI. We find AI can improve ESG disclosure through automated processing and anti-greenwashing monitoring, yet generative AI may enable sophisticated symbolic compliance. AI offers opportunities for ESG disclosure and governance, but its actual effects depend on organizational incentives, disclosure environments, and accountability mechanisms.

title: The Algorithmic Authenticity Paradox: Creativity, Imitation, Authorship, and Human Agency in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: Preprint, Version 1.9. This conceptual paper examines a paradox in contemporary judgments of creative authenticity: highly imitative human cultural production can retain presumptive legitimacy, while disclosure of generative-AI involvement can reduce perceived creativity, value, or authorship even when substantial human agency remains. The paper synthesizes research across creativity studies, psychology, human-AI collaboration, platform culture, authorship, labor, and generative AI. It develops the Algorithmic Authenticity Paradox , proposes an eight-dimensional Agency-Transformation Framework for evaluating human contribution in AI-assisted creative processes, advances the Generative Scarcity Shift hypothesis, and derives six falsifiable propositions for future empirical research. Rather than treating either human provenance or AI participation as sufficient evidence of creativity, the paper argues for evaluating intentionality, consequential agency, transformation, evaluation, selection, integration, contextualization, and responsibility. Author: Derek Rasor, Independent Researcher Version: 1.9 Status: Preprint; not peer reviewed.

title: GENERATIVE AI IN MARKETING COMMUNICATIONS: IMPLICATIONS FOR BRAND DISTINCTIVENESS, CONSUMER TRUST, AND REGULATORY DISCLOSURE.
abstract: This review examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping brand communications, with a particular focus on distinctive brand assets (DBAs), authenticity, and persuasive outcomes. Following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and a PCC framework, primary empirical studies published between 2018 and 2025 were searched for across the Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO and the ACM Digital Library. A total of fourteen records met the eligibility criteria and were included in this study. Three key findings emerged across the reviewed studied. Firstly, the credibility, value and intentions of AI-involvement disclosure are typically diminished by manipulation/inauthenticity inferences, with the impact being moderated by audience traits and context. In addition to this, performance is fit-dependent. AI excels with agentic appeals and voice-category congruency, but underperforms in authenticity-intensive categories such as luxury. Consequently, synthetic spokesperson entities can function as DBAs when they are designed to be authentic, credible and trustworthy. There are several gaps in the evidence, including scarce field outcomes, limited measurement of distinctiveness and recognition, narrow disclosure manipulations, a Western and category bias, and a lack of preregistered replications. Overall, generative AI can enhance distinctiveness and performance when designed for congruence and transparency. However, unmanaged disclosure and misfit can erode brand authenticity and persuasion.

title: Misleading AI guidance in psychological publishing
abstract: In response to generative AI, SAGE, the Association for Psychological Science (APS), and the American Psychological Association (APA) have introduced policies to regulate its use in their journals. These policies share sensible aims—protecting confidentiality, preventing fabrication and plagiarism, preserving human accountability—but they also embed strong claims about large language models (LLMs). Such claims—often oversimplified and tied to particular deployments—anchor distinctions between “assistive” and “generative” use, set disclosure and citation rules, and justify blanket bans on entering content into AI systems. Using SAGE, APS, and APA guidance as a case study, I show how these claims propagate into policy rules and create recurring mismatches between underlying assumptions and stated requirements across six domains: capability claims, categorization, prohibited uses, confidentiality, disclosure, and attribution. Policies also disagree on basic issues such as whether routine AI‑assisted copyediting must be disclosed. I propose a mechanism‑ and risk‑based policy matrix that organizes AI use by material contribution to the scientific record and confidentiality risk, yielding four editorial stances. Applying this framework to APS and APA policies produces technology-agnostic language that preserves editorial aims while reducing disclosure burden, improving cross-journal coherence, and aligning AI guidance with current research practice.

title: Generated Luxury: How does the use of Generative AI affect Brand Perception of LuxuryAutomotive companies?
abstract: Artificial Intelligence and more specifically Generative AI presents newchallenges and opportunities to companies around the world. The luxury automotive industryis an ever growing one and eyes Generative AI adoption for use in marketing as well, but certaincharacteristics of customers and brands like need for emotional connection and authenticitymight create friction. The purpose of the study is defined as finding out how the use of Generative AI byluxury automotive companies is perceived by customers and how to preserve emotionalengagement and authenticity in its use. A systematic literature review was done to create a theoretical framework aroundbrand perception. An interpretivistic qualitative research design was employed to obtain elevenwritten interviews from luxury automotive customers. Thematic Analysis was used to findconcepts and themes that developed the initial theoretical framework and provide insight intocustomers’ perceptions. Answers are given to the two research questions, where the use of Generative AIby luxury automotive brands is perceived neutrally overall, and emotional engagement andauthenticity is preserved if there is disclosure and human involvement in the creation ofpromotional material. Managerial and academic implications are presented. Future areas ofresearch and discussion on research process are laid out.

title: Inspectable AI for Science: A Research Object Approach to Generative AI Governance
abstract: This paper introduces AI as a Research Object (AI-RO), a paradigm for governing the use of generative AI in scientific research. Instead of debating whether AI is an author or merely a tool, we propose treating AI interactions as structured, inspectable components of the research process. Under this view, the legitimacy of an AI-assisted scientific paper depends on how model use is integrated into the workflow, documented, and made accountable. Drawing on Research Object theory and FAIR principles, we propose a framework for recording model configuration, prompts, and outputs through interaction logs and metadata packaging. These properties are particularly consequential in security and privacy (S&P) research, where provenance artifacts must satisfy confidentiality constraints, integrity guarantees, and auditability requirements that generic disclosure practices do not address. We implement a lightweight writing pipeline in which a language model synthesizes human-authored structured literature review notes under explicit constraints and produces a verifiable provenance record. We present this work as a position supported by an initial demonstrative workflow, arguing that governance of generative AI in science can be implemented as structured documentation, controlled disclosure, and integrity-preserving provenance capture. Based on this example, we outline and motivate a set of necessary future developments required to make such practices practical and widely adoptable.

title: Impact of Generative AI on Consumer Trust in Digital Advertising (focus on tools like Chat GPT) A Study in Thrissur District, Kerala
abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the landscape of digital advertising, enabling marketers to create highly personalized, scalable, and cost-efficient content. Tools such as Chat GPT allow the generation of human like advertising messages, raising critical concerns regarding consumer trust. Drawing on theories of consumer trust and technology acceptance, the research proposes a conceptual framework linking AI-generated content and consumer trust. The study also investigates the effects of AI disclosure and consumer AI literacy on these relationships. Respondents will be exposed to both AI-generated and human -created advertisements to assess differences in perception, followed by structured data collection. The research aims to investigate whether AI -generated advertisement enhance or undermine consumer trust and purchase intention.

title: Sorting the Harvest at Scale: A Governance Framework for Generative AI, from Brand Systems to Urban Futures
abstract: Preprint. Intended for submission to a peer-reviewed journal. Purpose. Generative AI's migration into urban design inherits, at much larger scale, an unresolved practitioner problem: how architects and planners evaluate, govern, and responsibly adopt AI tools before applying them to work of consequence. This paper asks whether a governance framework built at building and brand scale extends to the scale of generative urbanism. Methods. Practice-based research presents AI-KORP, a practitioner framework ("Basket & Ripeness") for auditing generative AI tools across brand, spatial, and process work. It tests it against two bodies of evidence: a proof-of-concept classification pipeline — AI-KORP | Neural Asset Archives — run first against a single building and then extended to aerial imagery of six logistics facilities at urban scale, yielding a three-type brand-architecture fusion typology; and the branded logistics landscape of Germany itself, in which national retail and delivery brands apply one colour and mark system across facade, fleet, and signage. Results. Brand and building recognition prove to be a single, fused visual layer rather than separate systems at both the building and city scales. An aerial survey of six German logistics facilities yields three distinct fusion types: fleet-carried signal with a neutral envelope (Type A), envelope-carried signal readable from altitude without the fleet present (Type B), and hybrid cases in which the envelope and the fleet carry the brand signal simultaneously across all layers (Type C). In all three types, the fusion precedes the classifier — it exists in the built environment before any AI system touches the imagery. Conclusions. Any credible framework for generative urbanism must specify not only what AI can generate, but also the ripeness, sovereignty, and disclosure conditions that must be met before generative or classification outputs are treated as design or planning authority — a governance-first, rather than capability-first, approach to scaling generative intelligence from the object to the city. Full methodology, code, and generated figures: https://github.com/archi-netizen/ai-korp-neural-archives

title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Evaluate the Quality of Chinese Environmental Information Disclosure in Chemical Firms
abstract: Environmental information disclosure plays a critical role in corporate sustainability, yet existing evaluation approaches often rely on subjective judgment or limited textual features. This study proposes a structured framework for assessing the environmental information disclosure quality (EIDQ) of chemical enterprises and develops a generative artificial intelligence (GAI)-driven automated scoring system to enhance evaluation consistency. Using 190 Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reports from 38 Chinese chemical firms between 2020 and 2024, we applied a multi-stage process combining indicator construction, DeepSeek-V3.2–based large language model (LLM) scoring, and cross-model validation. The results show that EIDQ exhibited a steady upward trend over the study period, reflecting a shift toward more quantitative and verifiable disclosure practices. The AI-generated scores demonstrated a high degree of alignment with human expert evaluations, and robustness tests confirmed the method’s transferability across different large language models. These findings provide methodological evidence for the feasibility of AI-assisted EIDQ assessment and offer practical implications for corporate sustainability reporting and regulatory oversight.

title: Generative AI and U.S. Financial Reporting Integrity: Detecting Narrative Manipulation, Risk Disclosure Gaming, and Fraud Signals in 10-K Filings
abstract: U.S. capital markets rely on high-integrity corporate disclosure, yet the narrative portions of annual reports—particularly Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) and Risk Factors—remain vulnerable to strategic language management and, increasingly, generative-AI-assisted drafting. Unlike traditional misstatement detection that focuses on accounting ratios, narrative manipulation can distort investor beliefs through selective emphasis, obfuscation, boilerplate recycling, and inflated forward-looking language while remaining difficult to audit at scale. This paper develops a conceptual–methodological framework to measure disclosure integrity and detect narrative manipulation in U.S. 10-K filings. We construct a transparent EDGAR pipeline that parses MD&A and Risk Factors and extracts auditable features capturing (i) financial-context tone and uncertainty, (ii) readability and complexity, (iii) risk-factor novelty versus boilerplate drift (year-to-year similarity), (iv) forward-looking intensity, and (v) “tone–fundamentals gaps” that flag potential inconsistency between narrative claims and contemporaneous performance signals. We benchmark interpretable statistical models (logit/elastic net) against flexible machine-learning specifications while preserving explainability, and we evaluate performance using governance-relevant outcomes including enforcement-linked misstatement events and restatement proxies, complemented by market-based reactions around filing dates. We further test whether narrative-risk signals strengthen in the period associated with broad diffusion of generative AI writing tools. The proposed framework contributes to accounting, finance, and regulatory technology by converting narrative disclosure risk into measurable, monitorable indicators. Findings are positioned to inform SEC disclosure oversight, audit planning, and issuer governance by enabling scalable detection of narrative manipulation and risk-disclosure gaming that may undermine investor protection and U.S. market integrity.
venue: Al-Kindi Center for Research and Development

title: A Framework for Trustworthy Healthcare AI
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping healthcare by supporting earlier diagnosis, assisting clinical decision-making, and improving operational efficiency. However, most systems remain deployed within human-in-the-loop workflows, limiting their impact and underscoring the need for greater automation grounded in trust and transparency. Despite widespread adoption of radiology AI, predictive analytics, and emerging large language models (LLMs), hospitals lack a standardized framework to evaluate fairness, reliability, accuracy, and real-world safety. Prior failures illustrate how ambiguous objectives and unvalidated proxy targets can produce inequitable outcomes and erode clinical trust. This paper argues for a unified evaluation framework capable of assessing both traditional classification models and generative LLMs via transparent reporting of performance markers, subgroup fairness analyses, and hallucination detection. Current FDA pathways provide a foundation, but they remain insufficient for governing continual-learning systems and generative models in clinical workflows. We propose that the FDA extend these mechanisms to require mandatory disclosure of training data provenance and standardized benchmarks for clinical safety and relevance. Establishing such a framework is crucial to ensure that AI advances deliver autonomously safe and trustworthy healthcare. Keywords: healthcare AI, evaluation framework, algorithmic bias, FDA regulation, large language models, trustworthy AI

title: Generative AI in Qualitative Research and Related Transparency Problems: A Novel Heuristic for Disclosing Uses of AI
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models (LLMs), are rapidly transforming qualitative data analysis by offering unprecedented speed and scale. However, this integration introduces significant challenges to methodological transparency due to the algorithmic opacity of these “black-box” systems and their hidden decision points. Traditional qualitative reporting guidelines predate generative AI and lack specific guidance for disclosing AI usage. This paper addresses this critical gap by introducing a novel heuristic framework that poses 20 questions across five key themes: The Research Team, Participant Interaction, Study Design, Data Practices, and Data Analysis, providing disclosure actions for each. This framework blends and augments existing frameworks, aligning with principles to guide researchers in meticulously documenting their AI-mediated analytic choices. Methodologically, the framework advances the field by requiring explicit reporting on: the roles of AI tools and the AI literacy of the human research team; AI’s involvement in participant communication, informed consent processes, and safeguards for sensitive demographic data; the alignment of AI tools with theoretical frameworks, their influence on sampling strategies, and discussions during IRB review; data storage, AI’s role in data creation (e.g., synthetic data, transcription, interview protocols), and its assistance in determining data saturation and participant checking; and the precise contributions of AI to coding and thematic categorization, alongside detailed documentation of iterative human-AI interactions and prompts used. By fostering rigorous audit trails and comprehensive documentation, the framework aims to maximize transparency, ensure methodological rigor, and uphold ethical standards in AI-augmented qualitative inquiry, thereby enhancing the credibility of findings.

title: The Asymmetry of Transparency — AI, Authors, and Academic Publishing
abstract: Academic publishers have responded to the rise of generative AI with an expanding apparatus of author disclosure requirements, yet they have imposed no corresponding obligations on themselves — neither regarding the use of AI in their own editorial workflows nor the licensing of scholarly content to AI providers. This asymmetry reflects a deeper structural imbalance in the author–publisher relationship, one that predates AI but that AI has brought into sharper relief. Current disclosure policies rest on an antiquated conception of originality, assume that composition rather than accountability defines authorship, and create perverse incentives that punish candor while rewarding silence. Detection tools compound the problem: they are unreliable, systematically biased against non-native English speakers, and lend unearned authority to consequential decisions. This essay argues that transparency, if it is to serve scholarly integrity, must be mutual. It proposes a framework grounded in collective negotiation of AI training rights, author responsibility for verification rather than process disclosure, collaborative best practices, and the embedding of norms within editorial infrastructure.

title: Generative AI in Academic Publishing
abstract: The authors present a qualitative comparative analysis of AI policies from five major academic publishers: Taylor & Francis, Elsevier, Sage, Wiley, and Springer Nature. They employed position statements of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) as their analytical framework. Six key themes emerged: permitted AI use, prohibited AI use, disclosure requirements, AI as author and co-author, AI in peer review, and policy adaptability. They found substantial differences among publishers in defining acceptable AI use and disclosure requirements. While all publishers explicitly state that AI cannot claim authorship, their policies differ in permitted AI roles, particularly regarding peer review and manuscript preparation. These inconsistencies create ethical challenges for authors and reviewers. The study concludes by recommending clearer, discipline-specific guidelines and enhanced reviewer training to ensure responsible AI use for upholding scholarly integrity.

title: Navigating the Landscape of Generative AI in Higher Education: Institutional Policies, Workforce Readiness, and Ethical Guidelines
abstract: This paper examines how higher education institutions are shaping emerging policies and guidelines surrounding generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). Drawing from 65 publicly available policy documents, the review identifies major themes such as data privacy, academic integrity, disclosure and attribution, tool vetting, intellectual property considerations, risk classification, and governance. In response to reviewer suggestions, the study now integrates profound global case studies from non-U.S. contexts, provides detailed, actionable recommendations for policy implementation, and separately discusses study limitations and the generalizability of the findings. By synthesizing core practices from a diverse array of universities, this paper offers a comprehensive framework that can serve as a blueprint for institutions worldwide seeking to refine or establish policies for the responsible deployment of generative AI.

title: Authorship Transparency Statement (ATS) Framework: A Technical Standard for the Multi-Tiered Disclosure of Generative AI in Creative Works
abstract: The Authorship Transparency Statement (ATS) is a comprehensive technical protocol designed to replace the primitive binary disclosure of AI—centered on the question "Did you use AI?"—with a nuanced, multi-tiered lexicon for creative synthesis. This framework provides an objective, methodology-based audit for creators, publishers, and legal institutions to accurately describe the degree of human-AI collaboration in any creative project. Abstract The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally disrupted the traditional concept of singular authorship, creating a critical nomenclature gap in the creative industries. Existing disclosure requirements frequently rely on low-resolution binaries that facilitate a "transparency paradox," wherein creators are incentivized toward obfuscation rather than honest methodology. This paper proposes the Authorship Transparency Statement (ATS) Framework, a multi-tiered technical protocol anchored by the Bright Line of Prose Origin. This mechanical distinction shifts the focus from subjective "creative control" to the objective origin of first-pass drafting. By defining a six-tier hierarchy (ATS-0 through ATS-5), the protocol categorizes the human role across a gradient of increasing AI autonomy: from the Traditional Artisan (ATS-0) and Architect (ATS-1) to the Director (ATS-3) and Systems Architect (ATS-4). Furthermore, the ATS framework provides the foundational schema for institutional implementation, offering standardized intake templates and machine-readable metadata structures designed to interoperate with emerging provenance standards such as C2PA. By replacing primitive binaries with a rigorous, methodology-based audit, the ATS protocol seeks to preserve the integrity of authorship and establish a verifiable "paperwork of becoming" for the new creative age. Key Features The Bright Line Principle: A mechanical threshold determining the boundary between reactive augmentation and generative synthesis. The 6-Tier Scale (0–5): A memorable, citable hierarchy of AI integration and human roles. The Extent Axis (E-Scale): A quantitative modifier (E0–E4) indicating the volume of AI involvement in a work. Multi-modal Support: Domain-specific interpretations for Research, Visual Arts, Music, Video, Code, and Data Assets. Technical Implementation: Machine-readable JSON and JSON-LD schemas for automated parsing and library indexing. Institutional Triage Logic: Ready-to-use policy bands for publishers and submission portals to automate legal and editorial reviews. Metadata & Implementation The official machine-readable schemas, validation tools, and community-driven edge-case rulings are maintained at the public repository:https://github.com/MeaningfulnessMediaGroup/ATS-Framework Protocol ID: ATS-FRAMEWORK-1.0License: CC-BY-4.0

title: Introducing LLM Calibration: Toward AI Reset Parameters and Behavioral Governance of Generative AI Systems
abstract: BackgroundRecent advances in large language models (LLMs) have significantly expanded the capabilities of artificial intelligence systems across domains such as education, healthcare, governance, and knowledge production. Despite these advances, LLMs continue to exhibit behavioral limitations including hallucinated outputs, epistemic overconfidence, inconsistent reasoning, and limited adaptability to institutional contexts. Existing mitigation strategies primarily focus on model training and alignment processes, providing limited mechanisms for regulating AI behavior during real-time deployment. ObjectiveThis study introduces the concept of LLM Calibration, a framework designed to regulate the behavioral dynamics of generative AI systems through configurable runtime parameters. The objective is to establish a conceptual foundation for behavioral governance mechanisms capable of improving reliability, contextual adaptability, and institutional compliance of large language models. MethodThe study develops a conceptual and interdisciplinary framework combining insights from artificial intelligence research, algorithmic governance, human–AI interaction, and digital platform economics. A taxonomy of calibration mechanisms is proposed, including behavioral calibration, epistemic calibration, institutional calibration, and adaptive calibration. The framework conceptualizes calibration as an intermediate governance layer positioned between user interaction interfaces and the underlying language model. ResultsThe proposed framework identifies several operational mechanisms through which LLM calibration could be implemented, including behavioral configuration parameters, uncertainty disclosure controls, and domain-specific calibration presets. The study further explores the potential emergence of calibration ecosystems in which behavioral presets could be distributed and configured across different institutional environments. Conclusion LLM Calibration represents a promising direction for improving the reliability and governance of generative AI systems. By introducing a behavioral governance layer capable of dynamically regulating model responses, this framework complements existing alignment techniques and opens new avenues for research in trustworthy AI. The article concludes by outlining a research agenda for the development of calibration benchmarks, evaluation metrics, and adaptive governance architectures for future generative AI systems.

title: Generative AI and Strategic Communication: Examining Its Impact on Organizational Communication Effectiveness and Public Trust
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become embedded in the strategic communication function, reshaping how organizations produce messages, engage stakeholders, and manage crises. Yet evidence on whether these capabilities strengthen organizational communication effectiveness or undermine public trust remains fragmented across disciplines. This article presents a systematic narrative literature review of twenty-five peer-reviewed studies published largely between 2022 and 2026, synthesizing findings from public relations, information systems, organizational behavior, and communication research. Using thematic synthesis, the review identifies four interrelated clusters: generative AI-enabled message production and personalization, algorithmic transparency and disclosure, trust calibration through tone and competence signaling, and organizational or institutional adaptation. Results show that efficiency and personalization gains are frequently offset by a transparency-trust paradox, whereby disclosing AI authorship can simultaneously legitimize and erode credibility depending on stakeholder AI literacy, message context, and institutional responsibility signaling. The novelty of this study lies in proposing an integrative Trust-Transparency-Effectiveness framework connecting micro-level message design, meso-level organizational practice, and macro-level public trust outcomes. The framework offers strategic communicators, corporate leaders, and policymakers a structured lens for deploying generative AI responsibly while safeguarding organizational legitimacy, stakeholder relationships, and public confidence in an increasingly algorithmically mediated communication environment.

title: The Case Analysis Integrity Gap: Generative AI, Cognitive Ownership, and Assessment Redesign in Management Education
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has created a substantial challenge for case-based management education. The case method is valued for developing diagnostic reasoning, decision-making under uncertainty, theoretical application, and persuasive communication. Yet, generative AI can now produce many of the visible outputs of case analysis, including problem diagnoses, strategic alternatives, and polished executive recommendations. This creates what we call the case analysis integrity gap: the divergence between the apparent quality of a submitted case analysis and the student's actual cognitive ownership of the underlying reasoning. The problem is not simply academic misconduct, though that is part of it. More fundamentally, generative AI erodes the relationship between the submitted product and the learning it is supposed to represent. Drawing on experiential learning theory, cognitive offloading, and authentic assessment, we develop a conceptual framework that distinguishes AI-augmented case learning (in which students retain ownership of the central judgment) from AI-substituted case analysis (in which AI performs the core diagnostic and reasoning work). We propose assessment redesign principles, including staged submissions, disclosure of AI use, an oral defense, and a critique of AI-generated outputs. The paper shows how case pedagogy can be restructured to preserve assessment validity while equipping students for AI-enabled managerial practice.

title: MedBuild AI: An Agent-Based Hybrid Intelligence Framework for Reshaping Agency in Healthcare Infrastructure Planning through Generative Design for Medical Architecture
abstract: Preprint describing MedBuild AI, an agent-based hybrid intelligence framework that integrates LLM-driven conversational data collection, rule-based program synthesis, and procedural 3D layout/model generation for low-resource healthcare facility planning. The work targets human-in-the-loop, participatory workflows in healthcare architecture and computational design, with reproducible web demo: https://intro-dot-medbuildai.uc.r.appspot.com/ . Disclosure: This is a non-peer-reviewed preprint intended for rapid dissemination and citation. The manuscript is under submission to a peer-reviewed venue; upon acceptance, the journal DOI will be added here.

title: Designing AI-Aware Assessment in Higher Education: A Cross-National Analysis of Generative AI Guidance and Design Patterns in English-Medium Universities
abstract: Generative AI is reshaping coursework and assessment in higher education, yet institutional guidance still varies in how clearly broad principles are translated into assessment practice. Guided by pattern-based educational design, the study used a framework-based document analysis of 21 official, public-facing institutional and teaching-unit guidance documents from universities in Europe, North America, Australasia, and Asia. The analysis combined directed qualitative coding with descriptive cross-case summaries of permitted and prohibited uses, disclosure and verification requirements, ethical safeguards, and ratings of clarity, actionability, and assessment specificity. Assessment-related configurations were synthesised into recurrent design patterns, and a descriptive ethical gap map compared the presence or absence of provisions related to privacy, consent, retention, fairness, and accessibility. Across the corpus, all universities allowed some student use of generative AI under conditions, and almost all required disclosure. Policies were generally clear, actionable, and assessment-specific. Four patterns were especially prominent: (1) process-evidence portfolios with AI-use logs, (2) AI-assisted drafting plus in-class or oral verification, (3) critical engagement with AI outputs, and (4) secure high-stakes exams combined with AI-enabled coursework. The ethical mapping showed stronger attention to public-upload risks and bias awareness than to data retention, consent language, and accessibility alternatives. Overall, the findings suggest that universities in this purposive sample have moved beyond blanket prohibition toward more assessment-aware guidance, while important governance and equity gaps remain. The resulting pattern library is offered as a provisional, policy-grounded resource for translating high-level AI principles into concrete assessment design options.

title: Research on the Competition Law Risks and Regulation Brought by Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The emergence of chatGPT signifies that Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies for generating content will have a significant impact on people’s work and lifestyle. Nowadays, R&D of generative AI such as chatGPT has become the core domain in the latest wave of technological competition among nations, yet we must be aware that it may result in the disclosure of trade secrets, abuse of dominant market position and other market competition and monopoly risks. In order to regulate the advancement of generative artificial intelligence, it is imperative to refine the existing legislative framework and establish a novel regulatory architecture that involves the participation of the government, corporations, and end-users, to ensure both the free development of technology and its orderly compliance, and guard against the occurrence of malicious competition and market monopolies.

title: A Scoping Review of Thirteen Claims on Recorded versus Declared Verification of AI Use in Research: Protocol
abstract: This registration records the protocol for a scoping review, declared before any database search has been executed. Background. Research integrity currently depends on individual conscience: authors are asked to declare their use of AI, and there is no mechanism by which such a declaration can be verified. The largest available measurement of practice found 76 AI disclosures across 75,172 papers (He and Bu, 2026, PNAS), in journals with disclosure policies in force, against independent bibliometric estimates placing LLM involvement above 10% of 2024 papers. This work proceeds from the observation that integrity questions divide into two classes: those a record can settle — sources retrieved, dates, parameters, tool and data versions — and those no record can reach, such as understanding, judgement, and whether an argument is warranted. It proposes that mandatory disclosure be confined to the second class while the first is met by verifiable process records. Objective. To map the existing evidence bearing on thirteen claims arising from that position, and to determine which are already established in the literature, which are contested, and which are unexamined. Design. A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. A scoping review is the appropriate instrument because the question asks what evidence exists across a broad and recent field rather than what a defined body of evidence concludes about a defined intervention; the thirteen claims are heterogeneous — some empirical, some conceptual, some normative — and no single outcome measure spans them. No meta-analysis and no risk-of-bias assessment will be conducted, neither being required for a scoping review. PROSPERO does not accept scoping review protocols, which is why this registration is made here. Framework (PCC). Population: researchers, authors, editors, reviewers and integrity bodies in scholarly publishing. Concept: disclosure, verification and provenance of AI use in research. Context: peer-reviewed scholarly publishing and its governing standards, across disciplines and regions, 2018 onward. Sources. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, LISTA, ERIC, PubMed, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, arXiv and medRxiv, together with named policy sources (COPE, ICMJE, WAME, ISC/WCRI, and major publisher AI policies) located by direct navigation. Full Boolean strings, eligibility criteria, the citation-chaining seed set, the data-charting form and the ten items to be recorded at the time of searching are specified in the attached protocol. The thirteen claims are reproduced in full in its Appendix. Expected outcomes. A PRISMA-ScR flow diagram, a charted evidence table, and a claim-by-claim assignment of each of the thirteen claims to one of three states: established, contested, or unexamined. Novelty is therefore an output of this review rather than an assumption behind it; no claim of novelty is made in advance. Intended reporting venue: Learned Publishing. Declared limitations. Single reviewer, no funding, no research assistance; English-language sources only; and the fact that no current infrastructure emits the process records the underlying framework describes, so every recorded item will be captured manually and incompletely. That last constraint is itself an instance of the condition the work examines, and will be reported as a finding rather than concealed. AI use. The exploratory work preceding this protocol was conducted with AI assistance and is documented separately in an accompanying provenance record, which audits it against the standard proposed here and reports that it fails on ten of nineteen items. That work is explicitly not part of this protocol and will be treated as a specimen for audit, not as a source of evidence. Permitted and prohibited AI uses under this protocol are declared in its Section 7.

title: GiriNeoAIMisc™: NICU AI Governance Decision Support System for Audit, Quality Improvement, Ethics and Medicolegal Risk
abstract: GiriNeoAIMisc™ is a single-file, offline governance decision support system for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). It helps NICU leads, neonatologists, nurses, quality and audit officers, ethics committees and hospital administrators to evaluate, deploy, audit and, when needed, retire AI tools safely. Modules: (1) Audit: AI for clinical audit and audit of AI itself (medical algorithmic audit), with post-deployment monitoring grouped as Performance, Safety, Equity and Workflow, a local performance calculator with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, and an observed-to-expected mortality ratio for internal trend review. (2) Quality improvement: Model for Improvement adapted for AI, evidence-maturity table of NICU AI applications, a sepsis early-warning worked example and a reporting-standard selector (SQUIRE 2.0, TRIPOD+AI, TRIPOD-LLM, DECIDE-AI, CONSORT-AI, FUTURE-AI). (3) Ethics: eight NICU AI ethical domains, parent and staff perspectives, an ethics-review and consent pathway helper, a parent communication script and a documentation-language check. (4) Medicolegal: Indian framework (standard of care, BNS 2023, Consumer Protection Act 2019, DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025 including the limits of the health-service exemption for children's data, CDSCO medical device software guidance 2026, ICMR and MeitY guidance) with global reference points (EU AI Act as amended in 2026, US FDA, IMDRF, WHO), a liability scenario navigator and an AI-use documentation note generator. The GiriNeoAI-READY assessment uses five go/no-go gates (local validation, named accountable owner, monitoring and rollback plan, DPDP-compliant data flow, traceability) plus a stop rule, and nine descriptive maturity enhancers; it informs, but does not authorise, deployment decisions, which rest with a NICU AI stewardship group. The tool also provides consequence tiers, a stewardship structure, an AI governance register, printable checklists, root-cause questions, CME (8-question self-assessment, team drill) and FAQs. Evidence reviewed through 27 September 2026; 53 Vancouver references. Supportive signal, not a directive; not legal advice; not for clinical decisions about individual patients. Part of the GAIR Innovation Registry, governed by the GIRISH-M™ architecture.

title: Visual Secondhand Scrolling in Shared Environments: A Conceptual Framework and Experimental Protocol for Involuntary Exposure to Short-Form Video
abstract: Concept paper / proposed experimental protocol. Not peer reviewed. No completed experiment is reported. Short-form video research has focused primarily on people who intentionally use the platforms. Less is known about bystanders who can see another person's rapidly changing feed without selecting, controlling, or intending to consume it. This concept paper defines visual secondhand scrolling (VSS) as incidental or involuntary visual exposure to rapidly changing digital content displayed on another person's device while the observer is engaged in another activity. The phrase “secondhand scrolling” is not presented as novel: it appeared in public writing by 2021 and 2023, and a 2026 human-computer interaction preprint used it for ambient technology exposure in the context of misophonia. The narrower contribution proposed here is an operational visual-attention framework for silent, neighboring short-form feeds. Existing studies show that task-irrelevant visual events and motion can capture attention under some conditions, and experimental studies of active short-form-video use report acute prospective-memory effects. Those findings do not establish an equivalent effect in passive observers. This paper therefore specifies testable hypotheses, a candidate exposure construct—visual secondhand scroll exposure (VSSE)—and a controlled eye-tracking protocol comparing screen-off, static, long-form, and short-form neighboring-screen conditions. The primary proposed outcome is neighboring-screen gaze time; task performance and subjective distraction are secondary outcomes. No medical injury, diagnosis, or long-term cognitive effect is claimed. The manuscript includes an AI-assistance disclosure.

title: Geometry of Neural Coding as a Computational Substrate: How Hyperbolic Manifolds, Chaotic Regularization, Compositional Fixed Points, Burst-Gated Goals, Metastable Segmentation, and Multifractal Criticality Jointly Constrain a Candidate Framework for Population-Level Neural Computation
abstract: This version (2026-09-26) corrects a citation error found by an automated check and confirmed by hand against the arXiv abstracts. Version 2 cited the identifier 2606.04428, an unrelated astrophysics paper on fast-spinning black holes, for the theoretical framework in which chaotic recurrent dynamics produce local roughness with global smoothness and act as an intrinsic regularizer of neural representations. That framework is arXiv:2606.04426 ("Discrete signaling mediates chaotic regularization in recurrent neural networks"), and every citation to it is corrected. The thesis is unchanged. This version has not had a full claim-by-claim audit. The full list of corrections is at the top of the PDF. A central question in computational neuroscience is not merely what neural populations encode, but how the geometric and dynamical structure of those populations enables computation. This paper synthesizes six recent findings from the q-bio.NC corpus to argue that neural population geometry is not an epiphenomenon of encoding but a candidate computational substrate in its own right. Specifically, we examine: (1) theoretical evidence that hippocampal population activity may induce hyperbolic geometry, yielding expanded associative memory capacity and improved decoding accuracy arXiv:2606.10238; (2) a framework suggesting that chaotic recurrent dynamics produce local roughness with global smoothness, potentially acting as an intrinsic regularizer of population codes arXiv:2606.04426; (3) a formal proof that inhibition-dominated threshold-linear networks support compositional fixed-point structure via low-rank inter-module couplings, with the complete characterization established for rank-1 gluings arXiv:2606.07336; (4) empirical and modeling evidence that burst fraction in macaque motor cortex is proposed to encode goal information via a bilinear gate implemented by layer-5 pyramidal dendrites arXiv:2606.10891; (5) a review synthesizing event segmentation and metastable neural states into a unified account of temporally nested cognitive computation, connecting to our thesis primarily through conceptual analogy rather than new empirical data arXiv:2605.31473; and (6) multifractal criticality measures from sleep EEG in a women-only longitudinal cohort that predict future cognitive decline, supporting the Brain Criticality Hypothesis as a systems-level constraint arXiv:2606.10889. This is a heuristic reading, not a derivation: the six findings do not share a common formal structure, but they converge on the hypothesis that geometry, dynamics, and modularity are jointly necessary, not individually sufficient, for flexible neural computation. The falsification path for the overall thesis is stated in the Synthesis section for each claim and in the Discussion. Sources are drawn from the q-bio.NC primary category; the corpus pool contained approximately 80 papers across q-bio.NC and cs.CL. All sources are arXiv preprints and have not undergone peer review at the time of this synthesis. Authorship: Saluca Agentic AI Research Team (Saluca LLC). title: Semantic Progress, Neural Alignment, and the Geometry of Shared Representations: A Candidate Framework for How Information Accumulation Constraints Are Shared Across Brains and Language Models
abstract: This version corrects a wrong arXiv identifier. Version 2 cited the theoretical paper on chaotic regularization in recurrent neural networks, "Discrete signaling mediates chaotic regularization in recurrent neural networks", as arXiv:2606.04428 in six places, including item 3 of the abstract. That identifier belongs to an unrelated astrophysics paper; the correct identifier is arXiv:2606.04426, and all six citations are corrected. What the text says about the paper matches its abstract, so no claim changes. An internal reference in the selection criteria is reworded, typographic dashes are removed, the Greek letter eta now renders in the PDF, and the file carries a neutral name. The abstract below differs from version 2 only in that citation and in punctuation. The error was found by an automated check and confirmed by hand against arXiv; this version has not had a full claim-by-claim audit. A recurring structural pattern appears across recent work in computational neuroscience and natural language processing: the accumulation of new, non-redundant information over sequential inputs is governed by measurable geometric and information-theoretic constraints that appear to operate similarly, though not identically, in human neural systems and large language models (LLMs). This paper synthesizes six to seven findings from recent arXiv preprints (primary categories: q-bio.NC and cs.CL) to articulate a candidate framework we call semantic accumulation geometry: the hypothesis that the rate and structure of information gain over sequential inputs is constrained by representational geometry, and that this constraint produces measurable alignment between neural and model-derived accounts of meaning. Specifically, we draw on evidence that (1) LLMs selectively converge with human-shared neural semantic representations along specific semantic dimensions rather than globally arXiv:2606.11598; (2) semantic progress in multi-turn dialogue can be formalized as question-conditioned uncertainty reduction with tractable geometric structure arXiv:2606.12332; (3) chaotic recurrent networks produce smooth population codes through intrinsic regularization, providing a mechanistic substrate for stable representational geometry arXiv:2606.04426; (4) speech foundation models exhibit hierarchical brain alignment that is temporally structured rather than static arXiv:2606.02305; (5) hyperbolic geometry in hippocampal population activity may confer capacity and decoding advantages consistent with the demands of accumulating structured information arXiv:2606.10238; (6) the policy compression framework, when extended to include irreducible uncertainty costs, reframes cognitive cost as a joint function of complexity and conditional entropy arXiv:2606.13132; and (7) sparse autoencoder representations of neural activity obey optimality constraints that produce hierarchical feature structure arXiv:2606.02385. This is explicitly a heuristic reading, not a derivation: the sources share vocabulary and structural analogies but do not share a common formal apparatus. Falsification paths are named for each major claim. The framework is offered as a candidate structural pattern worth investigating, not a paradigm-level claim. title: Categorical Symmetry as Phase Organizer: How Non-Invertible Symmetries, Fusion Categories, and Generalized Gauging Classify Beyond-Landau Transitions in One and Two Dimensions
abstract: This version corrects two citation errors. Six passages cited the identifier 2605.31856, which does not exist on arXiv; the passages describe arXiv:2606.05856 (Understanding deconfined quantum critical points from crystalline categorical Landau paradigm), and all six now cite it. An excluded paper on quantum thermal logic gates was listed under the wrong identifier and now carries its correct one, arXiv:2606.06432. The wording of the claims is unchanged. This version corrects specific citation errors found by an automated check and confirmed by hand; it has not had a full claim-by-claim audit. The full list of corrections is at the top of the PDF. The Landau paradigm organizes phases of matter by the spontaneous breaking of invertible symmetries, with order parameters valued in representations of ordinary groups. A cluster of recent preprints in cond-mat.str-el suggests, through complementary microscopic and categorical analyses, that this framework is insufficient even in principle for a broad class of transitions: those governed by non-invertible symmetries, whose fusion rules do not close in a group but in a richer algebraic structure called a fusion category. This paper synthesizes six primary findings from that corpus into a candidate structural reading, explicitly a heuristic unification, not a derivation from a single formalism, of how categorical symmetry data organizes gapped phases, critical points, and order parameters beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. The core thesis is as follows. (1) Gapped phases in 1+1d and 2+1d are classified not by which symmetry group is broken, but by which Lagrangian algebra in the Drinfel'd center of the symmetry category is preserved in the ground-state subspace. (2) Deconfined quantum critical points (DQCPs) arise generically when gauging an anomalous invertible symmetry produces a non-invertible dual, and the resulting transition is dual to spontaneous breaking of that non-invertible symmetry. (3) Twin phases, inequivalent gapped phases sharing identical anyon content and ground-state degeneracy, are the categorical signature of transitions that are intrinsically beyond Landau even after all possible gaugings. (4) These structures are not merely formal: they are realized in concrete lattice models, including Rydberg spin chains and spin-1/2 chains with D8 and H8 symmetry, where numerical DMRG and exact diagonalization confirm the predicted critical theories. Claim (5), that non-invertible symmetry-enriched topological order requires a relative-center construction, is treated as a speculative bridge between two formalisms whose equivalence is not established in the abstracts, and is placed in a weakly-connected addendum (§A). The primary falsification path is numerical: a DMRG or quantum Monte Carlo study of the dimer-to-ferromagnet transition in the D8 spin chain (arXiv:2606.06343, arXiv:2606.05856) should find central charge c ≈ 1 and confirm that no local order parameter distinguishes the two sides after gauging, if either condition fails, the categorical classification is incomplete. Sources are drawn from cond-mat.str-el (six papers), with additional papers noted but not incorporated into the main synthesis (see §4.2 and §A).
